name: NVIDIA-Certified Professional: Agentic AI
audience: AI engineers with 1–3 years in AI/ML and hands-on production agent projects

lessons.title: Reactive, deliberative and hybrid agents, and the ReAct loop
lessons.summary: How the three classic agent architectures trade speed for foresight, and how the ReAct Thought, Action, Observation loop turns an LLM into a deliberative agent that grounds its reasoning in tool results.

sections.heading: Three architectures, one trade-off
sections.body:
The NCP-AAI study guide expects you to know **reactive, deliberative and hybrid** architectures and to pick between them for a scenario.

| Architecture | How it decides | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reactive** | Stimulus maps straight to response (rules, a classifier, a single prompt). No planning, no world model. | Fast, cheap, predictable | Shallow: cannot pursue multi-step goals |
| **Deliberative** | Builds or consults a model of the goal and world, plans, then acts | Handles multi-step goals and novel situations | Slower, costlier, more ways to go wrong |
| **Hybrid** | A reactive layer handles time-critical inputs; a deliberative planner sits above it | Fast reflexes *and* long-horizon goals | More components to design and test |

Exam scenarios usually hide the answer in a constraint. A hard latency budget plus a safety reflex (stop the robot, block the transaction) points to a reactive layer. A goal that needs several dependent steps points to deliberation. If both appear in one scenario, the answer is hybrid.

sections.heading: Matching architecture to the job
sections.body:
- A **FAQ bot** with a fixed set of intents does not need a planner. A reactive design (intent classifier plus templated or single-prompt answers) is cheaper and more reliable.
- A **research assistant** that must search, read, compare and write needs deliberation: each step depends on what the previous step found.
- A **warehouse or factory agent** that must halt instantly on a sensor alarm but also schedule multi-step work is the classic hybrid.

Adding deliberation where it is not needed is a common anti-pattern. Every extra reasoning step adds latency, tokens and a chance to drift.

sections.heading: The ReAct loop
sections.body:
**ReAct** (Reason + Act) interleaves reasoning traces with tool calls ([Yao et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)):

1. **Thought**: the model reasons about what it knows and what it needs next.
2. **Action**: it emits a tool call (a tool name plus arguments).
3. **Observation**: the runtime executes the tool and appends the result to the context.
4. Repeat until the model emits a final answer.

The point of the loop is **grounding**. Each observation is real data the next thought must account for, which reduces hallucination compared with reasoning alone. It also produces a readable trace you can show to users and use for debugging.

Engineering controls every ReAct agent needs:
- a **maximum iteration** cap and a clear stop condition, so a confused agent cannot loop forever;
- **tool-error handling** that returns the error as an observation instead of crashing the run;
- **output parsing** that tolerates or repairs malformed tool calls.

sections.heading: ReAct relatives you should recognise
sections.body:
- **ReWOO** plans all tool calls up front, executes them, then solves. It needs fewer LLM calls than ReAct when the plan does not depend on intermediate results ([ReWOO paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323)). It adapts poorly when an early result should change the plan.
- **Reflection / self-critique** adds a step where the agent reviews its own output and retries.
- **Plan-and-execute** separates a planner from an executor and re-plans on failure.

The NeMo Agent Toolkit (NAT) ships ready-made agent types for several of these: **ReAct**, **ReWOO**, **Reasoning**, **Router**, **Tool Calling**, and **Sequential** and **Parallel Executor** agents, chosen through its YAML workflow configuration.

> **Current status:** NVIDIA deprecated the NeMo Agent Toolkit in October 2026 (end of life at the end of 2026) in favour of newer NeMo components. The exam study guide predates this and still tests NAT, so learn it as exam content.

keyPoints: Reactive = stimulus-response, no planning: fast but shallow.
Deliberative = plans toward goals over a world model: handles multi-step tasks, costs latency.
Hybrid = reactive layer for time-critical inputs plus a deliberative planner on top.
ReAct interleaves Thought, Action (tool call) and Observation until a final answer.
ReWOO plans every tool call first, so it uses fewer LLM calls but adapts less.
Every loop needs an iteration cap, a stop condition and tool errors fed back as observations.

gotchas.trap: Choosing a deliberative planner for a simple, fixed-intent FAQ bot because it is "more intelligent".
gotchas.correct: A reactive design is cheaper, faster and more predictable when there are no multi-step goals.

gotchas.trap: Thinking ReAct means the model reasons once and then calls all the tools.
gotchas.correct: That describes ReWOO. ReAct alternates reasoning and acting, and each observation shapes the next thought.

gotchas.trap: Letting a ReAct agent run until it decides to stop.
gotchas.correct: Always cap iterations and define termination, or a confused agent can loop on the same tool.

lessons.lab: Write a 30-line ReAct loop by hand with two tools (a calculator and a lookup dictionary). Log each Thought, Action and Observation. Then add a max-iterations cap and make one tool raise an error: confirm the agent sees the error as an observation and recovers. If you have the NeMo Agent Toolkit installed, compare your loop with its built-in ReAct agent type.

lessons.title: Prompt chains, logic trees and stateful orchestration
lessons.summary: When to hard-code control flow with prompt chains and routers, when to let a model choose, and how graph-based stateful orchestration with checkpoints makes multi-step, multi-turn agents reliable and resumable.

sections.heading: A spectrum of control
sections.body:
Study-guide objective 1.6 asks you to apply **logic trees, prompt chains and stateful orchestration** for multi-step reasoning. Think of them as a spectrum from "the developer decides the path" to "the model decides the path":

1. **Prompt chain**: a fixed sequence of LLM calls where each output feeds the next (extract, then validate, then format). Predictable, easy to test, cheap.
2. **Logic tree / router**: a classifier or rule picks a branch (billing chain versus technical-support chain). Still developer-defined paths, but chosen per input.
3. **Agent loop**: the model chooses the next tool or step at runtime (ReAct). Flexible but less predictable.

Use the least autonomy that solves the problem. If you can draw the flowchart in advance, a chain or router usually beats a free-roaming agent on reliability, cost and testability.

sections.heading: Making chains reliable
sections.body:
- Put **validation gates** between steps: check the output schema, required fields or a simple rule before passing it on. Fail fast or retry the step rather than letting a bad intermediate result poison later steps.
- Give each step **one job** and a focused prompt. A single mega-prompt that extracts, reasons and formats at once is harder to debug.
- Make branches explicit. A router should have a defined fallback branch (for example, a human handoff) for inputs it cannot classify.

In NAT, the **Sequential Executor** runs steps in order, the **Router** agent dispatches to one of several branches, and the **Parallel Executor** fans independent steps out at once.

sections.heading: Stateful orchestration as a graph
sections.body:
Framework-neutral mental model (LangGraph-style):

- **Nodes** are steps: an LLM call, a tool, a sub-agent or a human review.
- **Edges** carry control flow. **Conditional edges** branch on state, for example "if the validator failed, go back to the drafter".
- A **shared state** object travels through the graph and accumulates results.
- **Cycles** are allowed, which gives you retry and reflection loops (bounded by a counter).
- The state is **checkpointed** after each step, keyed by a thread or session ID.

Checkpointing is what makes an agent **stateful across turns and failures**:
- a multi-turn task can pause for user input and resume later from the same point;
- a crash or timeout resumes from the last checkpoint instead of restarting;
- a human-approval step can **interrupt** the graph and resume when the reviewer responds;
- the saved states form an audit trail of how the agent reached its result.

sections.heading: Memory belongs in the design
sections.body:
The study guide also lists **short- and long-term memory** under this domain (1.4) as well as in Cognition, Planning and Memory.

- **Short-term memory** is the working context: the current conversation and graph state. Manage it with trimming, sliding windows or summarisation so long sessions stay inside the context window.
- **Long-term memory** persists outside the model across sessions: past interactions (episodic), facts (semantic, often in a vector or graph store) and learned procedures. It is retrieved into context when relevant.

Design decision: what does the agent need to remember *within* this task (state) versus *across* tasks (long-term store)? Mixing the two, for example stuffing every past conversation into the prompt, is a cost and accuracy anti-pattern.

keyPoints: Prompt chain = fixed sequence; router/logic tree = developer-defined branches; agent loop = model picks the path.
Use the least autonomy that solves the task: chains are cheaper and easier to test.
Put validation gates between chain steps and a fallback branch on every router.
Graph orchestration: nodes, conditional edges, shared state, bounded cycles.
Checkpointing state per thread ID enables multi-turn resume, crash recovery and human interrupts.
Short-term memory = working context; long-term memory = external store retrieved when relevant.

gotchas.trap: Replacing a well-understood, fixed workflow with a fully autonomous agent.
gotchas.correct: If the path is known in advance, a prompt chain or router is more reliable, cheaper and testable.

gotchas.trap: Keeping multi-turn task state only in the LLM context window.
gotchas.correct: Persist orchestration state with checkpoints keyed by thread ID so the task survives restarts and long pauses.

gotchas.trap: Allowing unbounded reflection cycles in a graph.
gotchas.correct: Bound every cycle with a retry counter and exit to a fallback or human.

lessons.lab: Sketch a support-ticket graph: classify (router) to billing or technical branches, draft a reply, validate it against a checklist, loop back to the drafter at most twice, then require human approval for refunds. Mark which node writes which state fields and where a checkpoint lets the flow pause and resume.

lessons.title: Multi-agent orchestration and agent-to-agent communication
lessons.summary: The main multi-agent topologies, when splitting work across agents pays off, and how protocols such as A2A (agent to agent) and MCP (agent to tools and data) let independently built agents collaborate.

sections.heading: Why more than one agent
sections.body:
One agent with dozens of tools and a sprawling prompt tends to pick the wrong tool more often and becomes hard to test. Splitting work across **specialised agents** gives each a narrow prompt, a small toolset and its own evaluation. The cost is coordination overhead: more LLM calls, more latency and more failure modes. Split when specialisation or parallelism clearly pays for that overhead.

The study guide's reading list includes a multi-agent fraud-detection framework and NVIDIA's multi-agent blueprints (for example the Multi-Agent Intelligent Warehouse on build.nvidia.com), which are good mental models.

sections.heading: Topologies
sections.body:
| Pattern | Shape | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **Supervisor / orchestrator-worker** | A central agent delegates subtasks to workers and synthesises results | You need one accountable decision and an audit trail |
| **Hierarchical** | Supervisors of supervisors (teams) | One supervisor would juggle too many workers or too much context |
| **Sequential pipeline** | Agent A's output feeds agent B | Stages are fixed and ordered |
| **Parallel fan-out / fan-in** | Independent workers run at once, an aggregator merges | Subtasks do not depend on each other and latency matters |
| **Network / peer** | Agents message each other directly | Open-ended collaboration; hardest to control and debug |

Coordination concerns in every pattern: clear **task contracts** (input and output schema per agent), **timeouts and fallbacks** when a worker fails, loop limits on agents that hand work back and forth, and tracing across agent boundaries.

sections.heading: Agent-to-agent protocols: A2A
sections.body:
Objective 1.3 is about **configuring agent-to-agent communication protocols**. The open **A2A protocol** ([specification](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/)) is the main standard; version 1.0.0 is released and A2A has joined the Agentic AI Foundation.

- **Discovery:** each agent publishes an **Agent Card**, a JSON document at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` that lists its skills, capabilities (such as streaming and push notifications) and security schemes. Older material uses `agent.json`.
- **Core objects:** a **Task** (unit of work with an ID), **Messages** (turns from user or agent), **Parts** (content pieces) and **Artifacts** (outputs).
- **Task lifecycle:** Submitted, Working, then a terminal state (Completed, Failed, Canceled, Rejected) or an interrupted state (**Input Required**, **Auth Required**). Input Required is a protocol-level human-in-the-loop hook.
- **Transport:** JSON-RPC 2.0, gRPC and HTTP/REST bindings; streaming over server-sent events; push notifications to a client webhook for long tasks.
- **Opacity:** agents collaborate *without access to each other's internal state, memory or tools*. Each side can use a different framework or vendor.

sections.heading: A2A versus MCP
sections.body:
- **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** connects an agent or application to **tools, resources and prompts** exposed by a server.
- **A2A** connects an agent to **another agent**, treated as an opaque peer that accepts tasks.

Rule of thumb: if the other side is a function or data source your agent drives, expose it through MCP. If it is an autonomous agent that plans its own work, possibly owned by another team or company, talk to it over A2A. Many systems use both. The NeMo Agent Toolkit includes MCP client and server support and an A2A client and server, so a NAT workflow can both call remote agents and be published as one.

keyPoints: Split into agents when specialisation or parallelism outweighs coordination overhead.
Supervisor = central delegation and synthesis; hierarchical = teams of supervisors; fan-out = parallel independent work.
Every agent boundary needs a contract, a timeout, a fallback and tracing.
A2A: Agent Card discovery at /.well-known/agent-card.json, Tasks with a defined lifecycle, streaming and push notifications.
A2A agents are opaque: no shared internal state, memory or tools.
MCP = agent to tools and data; A2A = agent to agent.

gotchas.trap: Giving a remote partner agent direct access to your agent's memory store so they "stay in sync".
gotchas.correct: A2A is designed for opaque collaboration: exchange tasks, messages and artifacts, not internal state.

gotchas.trap: Using MCP to integrate another company's autonomous agent as if it were a stateless tool.
gotchas.correct: Use A2A for agent peers with their own planning and long-running tasks; use MCP for tools and data.

gotchas.trap: Adding agents to fix a problem a better prompt or one tool would solve.
gotchas.correct: Multi-agent designs add latency, cost and failure modes; justify each split.

lessons.lab: Design a fraud-review system with three specialist agents (transaction patterns, identity, device signals) and a supervisor. Write the input and output schema for each worker, the supervisor's fallback when a worker times out, and decide which external services are MCP tools and which partner capability would be reached over A2A. Draft the Agent Card fields you would publish for the supervisor.

lessons.title: Knowledge graphs, human-agent interfaces and scalable architecture
lessons.summary: Three design concerns that round out the domain: knowledge graphs for relational, multi-hop reasoning; interfaces that keep humans informed and in control; and architectures that adapt and scale.

sections.heading: Knowledge graphs for relational reasoning
sections.body:
Objective 1.7: **integrate knowledge graphs to enable relational reasoning.** A knowledge graph stores **entities** as nodes and **typed relationships** as edges (Supplier *supplies* Component, Component *used in* Product).

- **Vector search** answers "find text similar to this question". It is good for fuzzy, semantic lookups.
- **Graph queries** answer "follow these relationships": multi-hop questions such as *which products contain a part from a supplier in region X*. Similarity search often misses these because no single chunk contains the whole chain.
- **GraphRAG / hybrid** retrieval combines both: vector search finds entry points, graph traversal expands along relationships, and the results ground the LLM's answer.

Agents typically use the graph through a tool (a query function the agent can call) and can cite the path of relationships as an explanation.

sections.heading: Designing the human-agent interface
sections.body:
Objective 1.1 asks for **intuitive human-agent interaction**. Patterns that recur in exam scenarios:

- **Stream progress.** Stream tokens and surface intermediate steps ("searching orders...", "calling refund API") so users are not left staring at a spinner during multi-step runs.
- **Show your work.** Display the plan, sources and tool calls so users can check and trust the result.
- **Approval gates.** Before an irreversible or side-effecting action (refund, email, deletion), show what will happen and ask for confirmation.
- **Ask, do not guess.** When required information is missing, prompt the user (A2A's Input Required state and MCP's elicitation are protocol-level versions of this).
- **Easy escalation and correction.** Let users interrupt, edit, or hand off to a human, and collect structured feedback (ratings with reasons) to improve the agent.

NAT ships a built-in chat UI and an API server (`nat serve`) for exercising workflows interactively.

sections.heading: Adaptability and scalability
sections.body:
Objective 1.8: **ensure adaptability and scalability of the agent's architecture.**

Adaptability:
- Keep models, prompts and tools in **configuration**, not code, so you can swap an LLM or add a tool without a rewrite. NAT's YAML workflow configuration and its plugins for LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel and others are examples of a framework-agnostic approach.
- Put tools behind stable interfaces (function schemas, MCP servers) so their implementations can change independently.
- Version prompts, tools, model IDs and configs together so a change can be evaluated and rolled back.

Scalability:
- Make agent workers **stateless** and externalise state (checkpoints, memory, sessions) to a shared store, so any replica can serve any request and you can scale horizontally.
- Decompose by capability (router or supervisor plus specialists) so tool lists and prompts stay small as features grow.
- Run long or independent work **asynchronously** and in parallel; use streaming or push notifications for long tasks.
- Route easy requests to smaller, cheaper models and reserve large models for hard steps.

keyPoints: Knowledge graphs store entities and typed relationships; they answer multi-hop, relational questions that similarity search misses.
GraphRAG combines vector entry points with graph traversal.
Good agent UIs stream intermediate steps, show sources and tool calls, and gate irreversible actions behind approval.
Ask for missing information instead of guessing; give users interrupt, correct and escalate options.
Adaptability: config-driven models, prompts and tools behind stable interfaces, versioned together.
Scalability: stateless workers with externalised state, capability decomposition, async and parallel execution, model routing.

gotchas.trap: Using only a vector database for questions that require chaining several relationships.
gotchas.correct: Add a knowledge graph or GraphRAG so the agent can traverse relationships explicitly.

gotchas.trap: Hiding all intermediate activity to keep the UI "clean" during a long multi-step run.
gotchas.correct: Stream progress and expose the plan, sources and tool calls; it builds trust and lets users catch errors.

gotchas.trap: Storing session state in the memory of a single agent process and then adding replicas.
gotchas.correct: Externalise state to a shared store so requests can land on any replica.

lessons.lab: Model a small supply-chain knowledge graph (suppliers, components, products, regions) on paper or in any graph tool, then write the two-hop query for "products affected if supplier S fails". Next, mock up the agent UI for that question: where the plan, the graph path used as evidence and the "notify affected customers" approval button appear.

lessons.title: Prompt Chains and Multimodal Inputs
lessons.summary: How to write prompts that hold up in production, split work into dynamic prompt chains, and bring vision, speech and cross-modal embedding models into an agent.

sections.heading: Why prompts break in production
sections.body:
A prompt that works in a notebook often fails on real traffic. Inputs are messier, users phrase things in new ways, and one long prompt tries to do too many jobs at once. The study guide frames the skill as engineering prompts and **dynamic prompt chains for reliable performance**, so the goal is predictable behaviour, not clever wording.

The basic tools still apply:

- **A clear system prompt** that sets the role, the scope, the output format and what to do when unsure.
- **Few-shot examples** that match the exact output schema you expect.
- **Chain-of-thought** instructions for multi-step reasoning, with the reasoning kept apart from the final answer when the answer feeds code.
- **Structured output**: ask for JSON that matches a schema, then validate it in code and re-prompt on failure instead of trusting it.

sections.heading: Dynamic prompt chains
sections.body:
A **prompt chain** splits one large task into steps. Each step has its own focused prompt, and its checked output becomes the input to the next step. A typical chain is *extract → classify → retrieve → draft → check*.

A chain is **dynamic** when the next step is chosen at runtime from earlier outputs. For example, an intent classifier routes a billing question to a billing prompt and a tool-heavy path, while a greeting goes straight to a short reply. Stateful graph frameworks express this as nodes with conditional edges.

Why chains beat one big prompt:

1. Each step is smaller, so it is easier to test and debug.
2. You can **validate between steps** and stop or retry early.
3. You can pick a different model per step, such as a small fast model for classification and a larger one for drafting.
4. Failures point to one step, so you can trace them.

sections.heading: Prompt engineering vs p-tuning
sections.body: The guide includes NVIDIA's reading on *prompt engineering and p-tuning*. Prompt engineering changes only the text you send. **P-tuning** is a parameter-efficient method: a small model is trained to produce task-specific "virtual tokens" (soft prompt embeddings) that are prepended to the prompt, and at inference those virtual tokens come from a lookup table. The base model's weights stay frozen. Use it when good prompting has plateaued and full fine-tuning would cost too much. It is still a training step, so it needs labelled task data.

sections.heading: Integrating multimodal models
sections.body:
Domain 2 asks you to integrate generative and multimodal models for **text, vision and audio**. NVIDIA NIM covers these with model categories that include **Vision Language Models**, **Speech (Riva)** and **NV-CLIP**.

Common patterns:

- **Vision:** send images such as screenshots, charts or scanned forms to a VLM. It returns a description or structured fields, and a text LLM then reasons over that output.
- **Audio:** put speech recognition in front of the LLM and text-to-speech after it, streaming both ways to keep latency low for voice agents.
- **Cross-modal retrieval:** NV-CLIP puts images and text in a shared embedding space, so a text query can find relevant images.
- **Multimodal RAG:** the guide's reading pairs LlamaIndex, NIM and Milvus. Extract text, tables and images from documents, embed them, store the vectors, and retrieve across all of them at query time.

Keep each model behind its own interface, so you can swap a VLM or speech model without rewriting the agent.

keyPoints: Split overloaded prompts into a chain of focused steps with validation between them.
A dynamic chain chooses its next step at runtime from earlier outputs, for example with an intent router.
Ask for structured output and validate it against a schema in code. Never trust it blindly.
P-tuning learns soft-prompt embeddings while the base model stays frozen.
NIM model categories include VLMs, Speech/Riva and NV-CLIP for multimodal agents.

gotchas.trap: Adding more instructions to one giant prompt until it stops failing.
gotchas.correct: Break it into a chain so each step can be tested, validated and routed on its own.

gotchas.trap: Treating p-tuning as a kind of prompt wording.
gotchas.correct: P-tuning trains soft prompt embeddings while the model stays frozen. It needs data and a training step.

gotchas.trap: Pasting image bytes into a text-only LLM prompt.
gotchas.correct: Send images to a vision language model, or extract their content first, and give the text LLM structured results.

lessons.lab: Take a single prompt that extracts fields from a support email, classifies urgency and drafts a reply. Rewrite it as a three-step chain with a JSON schema check after extraction and a router after classification. Then compare failure rates on 20 sample emails.

lessons.title: Building Custom Tools and Functions
lessons.summary: Design tool schemas the model can call reliably, validate on the server, and register tools and functions in the NeMo Agent Toolkit so they can be reused across frameworks, MCP and A2A.

sections.heading: How tool calling works
sections.body:
In framework-neutral terms, the model does not run code itself. The loop goes like this:

1. The app tells the model which tools exist. Each has a **name**, a **description** and a **JSON Schema** for its arguments.
2. The model returns a structured call with a tool name and JSON arguments.
3. The app **validates** the arguments, runs the tool and returns the result to the model as an observation.
4. The model keeps reasoning, calls another tool or answers.

The ReAct pattern makes this an interleaved *Thought → Action → Observation* loop.

sections.heading: Designing tools the model calls correctly
sections.body:
Most wrong tool calls trace back to vague tool design. Good practice:

- **Specific names and descriptions** that say when to use the tool *and when not to*.
- **Tight schemas** using enums, formats, required fields and ranges instead of free-text strings.
- **Server-side validation** of every argument. Return a clear, structured error the model can act on, such as `date must be YYYY-MM-DD`.
- **Small, single-purpose tools** rather than one tool with a `mode` flag that does ten things.
- **Least privilege**: give tools only the permissions they need, and require human approval for irreversible side effects.
- **Idempotency** for write operations, for example an idempotency key, so retries cannot create duplicates.

sections.heading: Tools in the NeMo Agent Toolkit
sections.body:
The NeMo Agent Toolkit (NAT) registers tools as **Functions** or **Function Groups** (which can include per-user functions). It wires them together with a **YAML workflow configuration**, so you can change a workflow without changing code.

NAT also includes:

- **Framework plugins** for LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, AutoGen, Semantic Kernel, Agno, Google ADK and Strands. A tool written once can be used by agents in different frameworks.
- An **MCP client and server**. The client consumes tools from MCP servers, and the server publishes your functions as MCP tools.
- An **A2A client and server**, so other agents can delegate tasks to a workflow without seeing its internal tools or memory.
- Built-in agent types such as ReAct, ReWOO, Reasoning, Router, Tool Calling, and Sequential and Parallel Executors.

> **Current status:** NVIDIA deprecated NAT in October 2026, with end of life at the end of 2026. The study guide (SEP25) still tests NAT, under its earlier name Agent Intelligence Toolkit, so learn it as exam content.

sections.heading: MCP in one paragraph
sections.body: The Model Context Protocol uses JSON-RPC 2.0 between **hosts**, **clients** and **servers**. Servers offer **Tools** (functions the model runs), **Resources** (context and data) and **Prompts** (templated messages). Use MCP to connect an agent to tools and data. Use A2A to connect agents to other agents. The current revision (2026-07-28) is stateless: every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities, so older material describing a session handshake is out of date. Treat tool annotations from untrusted servers as untrusted.

keyPoints: The model emits a tool name plus JSON arguments. Your code validates and runs the tool.
Clear descriptions and constrained schemas reduce wrong calls. Server-side validation catches what remains.
Return tool errors as structured observations so the agent can recover.
NAT registers tools as Functions or Function Groups and composes workflows in YAML.
NAT provides MCP client/server and A2A client/server integrations plus multi-framework plugins.

gotchas.trap: Relying on the model to always send valid arguments because the schema is in the prompt.
gotchas.correct: Always validate arguments in the tool or server and return a clear error when they are invalid.

gotchas.trap: Using one generic tool with a free-text 'action' field.
gotchas.correct: Use small single-purpose tools with typed, constrained parameters.

gotchas.trap: Using A2A to give an agent access to a database tool.
gotchas.correct: MCP (or a direct function) connects agents to tools and data. A2A is for agent-to-agent delegation.

lessons.lab: Write a booking tool with a JSON Schema that uses an enum for room type and a date format. Register it as a NAT function in a workflow YAML, then send invalid arguments and confirm the agent gets a structured error and corrects itself.

lessons.title: Resilience, Streaming and Decision Strategies
lessons.summary: Apply retry, circuit breaker and fallback patterns to agent tool calls, stream responses and progress to users with feedback hooks, and refine how agents decide using evaluation data.

sections.heading: Retry done right
sections.body:
The study guide's Domain 2 readings include the Azure **Transient Fault Handling**, **Retry** and **Circuit Breaker** patterns. Agents call many remote services, including LLM endpoints, search APIs and business systems, so they hit transient faults all the time.

Retry rules:

- Retry only **transient** faults such as timeouts, 429s and 503s. Do not retry validation or auth errors, because the result will not change.
- Use **exponential backoff with jitter** so many clients don't retry at the same instant (a thundering herd).
- **Cap** the number of attempts and the total time.
- Retry only **idempotent or safe** operations. Protect writes with an idempotency key.

sections.heading: Circuit breakers and graceful recovery
sections.body:
A **circuit breaker** wraps calls to a dependency and has three states:

| State | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Closed** | Calls pass through and failures are counted. Too many failures trip it to Open. |
| **Open** | Calls **fail fast** without touching the dependency, for a cool-down period. |
| **Half-Open** | A limited number of trial calls go through. Success closes the breaker; failure opens it again. |

Combine the patterns so that retry logic **stops retrying while the breaker is open**. Otherwise retries keep hammering a dependency that is already down.

**Graceful degradation** means having a plan when a call still fails:

- Serve a cached answer.
- Fall back to a simpler or smaller model.
- Skip an optional enrichment step.
- Hand off to a human with the context attached.

Inside the agent loop, catch tool exceptions and return them as **structured observations**, so the model can choose another tool or re-plan instead of crashing. Bound the loop with a maximum number of iterations.

sections.heading: Streaming conversation flows with feedback
sections.body:
Long agent runs feel broken if the user sees nothing for 20 seconds. Two kinds of streaming help:

- **Token streaming**, usually over **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**, so the answer appears as it is generated.
- **Intermediate step events**, such as *Searching knowledge base…* or *Calling inventory API…*, which show progress and make the agent's behaviour visible.

Add feedback mechanisms to the flow. A thumbs up or down with a **reason code**, stored **with the trace** of that run, tells you exactly which step failed. Users should also be able to interrupt or correct the agent mid-stream.

sections.heading: Evaluating and refining decision strategies
sections.body:
Refining decisions is an evidence loop, not guesswork:

1. Build a dataset of representative tasks with expected answers. For tool-heavy agents, include expected tool trajectories too.
2. Run the agent. NAT supports this with `nat eval --config_file=...` and evaluators such as `trajectory` (an LLM judge of tool-use steps) and `ragas` metrics.
3. Use `--reps` to measure run-to-run variance before you trust a difference.
4. Change **one thing** at a time, such as a tool description, the router prompt or the agent type, and compare on the same dataset and the same judge.

The agent type is itself a strategy choice. **ReAct** re-decides after every observation, which makes it adaptive but costs more LLM calls. **ReWOO** plans all tool calls up front and then executes them, using fewer LLM calls when the tool sequence is predictable. A **Router** sends each request to a specialised path.

keyPoints: Retry only transient faults, with exponential backoff, jitter and a cap. Retry only idempotent operations.
Circuit breaker states are Closed, Open (fail fast) and Half-Open (trial calls).
Retries should stop while the breaker is open. Use fallbacks for graceful degradation.
Stream tokens over SSE and show intermediate step events. Attach feedback to traces.
Refine decisions with evaluation datasets, trajectory scoring and repeated runs. ReWOO uses fewer LLM calls than ReAct.

gotchas.trap: Retrying immediately in a tight loop until the call succeeds.
gotchas.correct: Use exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum number of attempts.

gotchas.trap: Retrying a failed 'create order' call without protection.
gotchas.correct: Make the write idempotent, for example with an idempotency key, or don't retry non-idempotent operations.

gotchas.trap: Comparing two agent versions on a single run each.
gotchas.correct: Use repeated runs on the same dataset and judge to separate real gains from variance.

lessons.lab: Wrap a flaky mock API in a retry decorator with jittered backoff and a circuit breaker. Simulate a 2-minute outage and check that calls fail fast while the breaker is open, that a cached fallback is served, and that the breaker closes after a successful half-open trial.

lessons.title: Evaluation pipelines with NeMo Agent Toolkit
lessons.summary: How to build a repeatable evaluation pipeline for an agent: a golden dataset, judge-based evaluators, `nat eval` run modes and the output files you read afterwards.

sections.heading: Why agents need an evaluation pipeline
sections.body:
An agent can reach the right answer by a bad route, or take a sensible route and still answer wrongly. A useful evaluation pipeline therefore checks two things:

- **Final-answer quality**: is the answer accurate, relevant and grounded in the retrieved context?
- **Trajectory quality**: did the agent choose sensible tools, in a sensible order, without wasted calls?

The pipeline has to be **repeatable**. That means a fixed dataset (often called a golden dataset), fixed evaluators and judge models, and a recorded configuration. Without those, a change in score could come from the agent, the judge or chance, and you can't tell which.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a `nat eval` run
sections.body:
NeMo Agent Toolkit (NAT) runs evaluation from the same YAML file that defines the workflow:

```bash
nat eval --config_file=workflow.yml
```

The `eval` section of the config has two parts:

- `eval.general` holds `output_dir`, `dataset`, `max_concurrency` (default 8) and the profiler settings.
- `eval.evaluators` has one named entry per evaluator. Each entry has a `_type` and, for judge-based evaluators, an `llm_name` that points to the judge LLM.

The dataset can be json, jsonl, csv, xls, parquet or a custom format. Its default columns are `id`, `question` and `answer`, where `answer` is the reference answer.

sections.heading: Built-in evaluators
sections.body:
| Evaluator `_type` | What it scores |
|---|---|
| `ragas` | RAG quality. The recommended metrics are **AnswerAccuracy**, **ContextRelevance** and **ResponseGroundedness**, each from 0 to 1. FactualCorrectness is also available. |
| `trajectory` | An LLM judge scores the agent's tool-use trajectory, meaning the sequence of steps and tool calls. |
| `tunable_rag_evaluator` | Coverage, Correctness and Relevance, with weights you can change or a custom judge prompt. |
| `langsmith`, `langsmith_custom`, `langsmith_judge` | Evaluators based on LangSmith. |

Run `nat info components -t evaluator` to list the evaluators installed in your environment.

sections.heading: Run modes worth knowing
sections.body:
- `--reps=N` repeats the whole run N times, so you can measure variance.
- `--override eval.general.max_concurrency 1` lowers parallelism, for example when a judge endpoint is rate-limited.
- `--skip_workflow --dataset=<file>` scores outputs that already exist, offline, without running the agent again.
- `--skip_completed_entries` resumes an interrupted run.
- `--endpoint http://localhost:8000` evaluates a remote workflow started with `nat serve`, not a local copy.

The NAT server also exposes an `/evaluate` REST endpoint, so evaluation can be started over HTTP.

sections.heading: Reading the outputs
sections.body:
Every run writes to `output_dir`:

- `workflow_output.json` holds what the agent actually produced for each dataset item.
- `<evaluator>_output.json` holds per-item scores and the judge's reasoning for each evaluator.
- `config_original.yml` is the config as you wrote it. `config_effective.yml` is the config **after** CLI overrides were applied. Use the effective one when you need to reproduce or audit a run. A `config_metadata.json` file is written alongside them.

If the profiler is turned on, its files go to the same directory (see the profiling lesson).

sections.heading: Current status of the toolkit
sections.body: > **Callout.** The study guide (dated SEP25) links to the *Agent Intelligence Toolkit* 1.1 docs. The same product was earlier called AgentIQ and is now the NeMo Agent Toolkit, with the `nvidia-nat` package and `nat` CLI since 1.2. NVIDIA deprecated NeMo Agent Toolkit in October 2026, with end of life at the end of 2026, and is moving to successor tools. The exam still tests NAT concepts, so learn `nat eval` as described here and check the NVIDIA docs for the current tooling in real projects.

keyPoints: Evaluate final answers and trajectories; a correct answer can hide a wasteful or unsafe route.
`eval.general` sets dataset, output_dir and max_concurrency (default 8); `eval.evaluators` lists each evaluator with `_type` and a judge `llm_name`.
Recommended ragas metrics: AnswerAccuracy, ContextRelevance and ResponseGroundedness, each scored 0 to 1.
`--skip_workflow` scores existing outputs offline; `--skip_completed_entries` resumes; `--endpoint` evaluates a served workflow; `--reps` measures variance.
`config_effective.yml` records the config after overrides, so use it for reproducibility.

gotchas.trap: Using `--skip_workflow` to evaluate a live deployed agent.
gotchas.correct: `--skip_workflow` only re-scores outputs already in the dataset. To evaluate a running `nat serve` instance, use `--endpoint`.

gotchas.trap: Reading `config_original.yml` to find out how a run was configured.
gotchas.correct: CLI overrides appear only in `config_effective.yml`.

gotchas.trap: Assuming one evaluator covers everything.
gotchas.correct: ragas scores answer and context quality, while `trajectory` scores the tool-use path. Use both for agents.

lessons.lab: Write a five-item jsonl dataset with `id`, `question` and `answer` for a small agent. Configure `ragas` and `trajectory` evaluators that share one judge LLM, run `nat eval` with `--reps=3`, then compare `config_original.yml` with `config_effective.yml` after adding an `--override`.

lessons.title: Comparing agents across tasks and datasets
lessons.summary: How to run fair, controlled comparisons between agent versions, measure variance, slice results by task and turn evaluation into a regression gate.

sections.heading: Control everything except the change
sections.body:
A comparison is only fair when the agent change is the **only** thing that differs between runs. Hold these constant:

- the same dataset, with the same items and reference answers
- the same evaluators and the same judge LLM and judge prompt
- the same concurrency and environment

If you give each agent its own judge, or a judge prompt tuned to its style, you are measuring the judges, not the agents. Keep `config_effective.yml` from each run so you can show what was held constant.

sections.heading: Measure variance before declaring a winner
sections.body:
LLM agents and LLM judges are both non-deterministic, so one run per version can mislead. A 0.03 gap between single runs may be noise.

Use `nat eval --reps=N` to repeat the run and look at the spread of scores for each version. Only treat a difference as real when it is larger than the run-to-run variation.

sections.heading: Slice by task and dataset
sections.body:
An aggregate score hides where an agent fails. Break per-item results from `<evaluator>_output.json` down by task category, dataset or difficulty. A version that improves the average while regressing a high-value slice, such as billing disputes in a support agent, may still be the wrong one to ship.

Compare across **several** datasets where you can, for example a curated golden set plus items drawn from recent production feedback, so a gain on one benchmark doesn't hide overfitting to it.

sections.heading: Answer metrics versus trajectory metrics
sections.body: Two agents with the same answer accuracy can differ a lot in cost and risk. Pair answer-level metrics (ragas AnswerAccuracy, ResponseGroundedness) with the `trajectory` evaluator and with profiler data such as tokens and latency. The best agent is the one that meets the quality bar at acceptable latency and cost, which is not always the one with the top accuracy score.

sections.heading: Evaluation as a regression gate
sections.body: Run the same `nat eval` job on a golden dataset in CI before promoting a new prompt, model or tool version. Promote only if key metrics don't regress beyond an agreed threshold. Version prompts, tool definitions, model IDs and configs together so a regression can be traced to the change that caused it.

keyPoints: Same dataset, same evaluators, same judge LLM and prompt: change only the agent.
Use `--reps` to measure run-to-run variance before trusting a small score gap.
Slice per-item results by task and dataset; averages hide regressions on important slices.
Weigh accuracy alongside trajectory quality, latency and cost.
Gate promotions with a CI eval run on a golden dataset.

gotchas.trap: Shipping version B because it beat version A by 0.02 in a single run.
gotchas.correct: Repeat runs (`--reps`) and check that the gap is larger than the variance.

gotchas.trap: Letting each team choose its own judge prompt for its agent.
gotchas.correct: Use one shared judge and prompt so scores are comparable.

gotchas.trap: Reporting only the overall average.
gotchas.correct: Report per-slice results so regressions on critical tasks are visible.

lessons.lab: Take two prompt variants of the same agent. Run each with `--reps=5` on one dataset and one judge, then compute the mean and spread per variant and per task category. Decide which to ship and write down the variance you observed.

lessons.title: Profiling, feedback and accuracy–latency–cost tuning
lessons.summary: Use the NAT profiler to find bottlenecks, collect structured user feedback and tune the accuracy, latency and cost trade-off with targeted, measured changes.

sections.heading: What the profiler collects
sections.body: The NAT profiler records tokens, latency and LLM and tool calls for each invocation, using framework callbacks. To instrument your own Python functions, decorate them with `@track_function`. The profiler runs as part of `nat eval`, so quality scores and performance data come from the same run.

sections.heading: Profiler options
sections.body:
These keys go under `eval.general.profiler`:

| Key | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `compute_llm_metrics` | Per-call LLM metrics such as latency and token counts |
| `token_uniqueness_forecast` | Forecasts how unique the tokens are across requests |
| `workflow_runtime_forecast` | Forecasts workflow runtime |
| `prompt_caching_prefixes` | Finds shared prompt prefixes that are candidates for KV-cache reuse |
| `bottleneck_analysis` | Finds where time goes, using `enable_nested_stack` or `simple_stack` |
| `concurrency_spike_analysis` | Flags moments when concurrency reaches or exceeds a `spike_threshold` |

Forecasts use linear and random-forest models. A separate Sizing Calculator, `nat sizing calc`, runs the workflow at several concurrency levels and estimates how many GPUs are needed for a target number of users and response time.

sections.heading: Profiler outputs
sections.body:
- `standardized_data_all.csv`: one row per profiled event, for your own analysis
- `workflow_profiling_report.txt` and `workflow_profiling_metrics.json`: summary and bottleneck findings
- `gantt_chart.png` (from bottleneck analysis; some versions prefix the model name): a timeline of LLM and tool calls that shows what ran in sequence and what ran in parallel
- `all_requests_profiler_traces.json`: raw traces
- `inference_optimization.json`: latency, throughput and runtime with 90%, 95% and 99% confidence intervals

sections.heading: Tuning accuracy against latency and cost
sections.body:
Common levers and what they cost you:

- **Smaller or quantized models** lower latency and cost but may lower accuracy. Route easy requests to a small model and keep the larger model for hard ones.
- **Fewer reasoning steps or tool calls** cut latency and tokens, but check with the `trajectory` evaluator and answer metrics that quality holds.
- **Prompt and KV caching** helps when many requests share a long prefix. `prompt_caching_prefixes` finds those prefixes.
- **Concurrency and batching** raise throughput, but watch p95 latency and spikes.

NAT also includes a hyper-parameter and prompt optimizer that searches configurations against your evaluation metrics. Whatever you change, re-run the same evaluation and compare against the baseline.

sections.heading: Structured user feedback
sections.body:
Free-text comments are hard to act on. Structured feedback is easier to use:

- thumbs up or down plus a **reason code** (for example wrong answer, missing source, too slow, unsafe)
- an optional rating and comment
- stored **with the trace or request ID**, so you can see exactly what the agent did

Review the negative cases, turn representative ones into new evaluation items, fix, and re-evaluate. This loop is often called a **data flywheel**. Don't retrain or change prompts automatically on raw feedback without review, because feedback is noisy and can be gamed.

sections.heading: From results to targeted optimisation
sections.body:
1. Find the biggest gap: a failing slice in the evaluator output, or the dominant span in the profiler report.
2. Form a hypothesis, for example "the retriever returns irrelevant chunks for billing questions" if ContextRelevance is low.
3. Change **one** thing.
4. Re-run the same evaluation, with `--reps`, and compare against the baseline on quality, latency and cost.

Changing several things at once, or optimising without a baseline, makes it impossible to say what helped.

keyPoints: The profiler records tokens, latency and LLM/tool calls per invocation; `@track_function` instruments custom code.
`bottleneck_analysis` and `gantt_chart.png` show where time goes; `prompt_caching_prefixes` finds KV-cache reuse opportunities.
`inference_optimization.json` reports latency, throughput and runtime with 90/95/99% confidence intervals; `nat sizing calc` estimates GPU needs for a target load.
Route easy requests to smaller models and confirm the accuracy impact with the same evaluation.
Structured feedback (reason codes plus trace IDs) feeds reviewed items back into the eval set.

gotchas.trap: Swapping every request to the smallest quantized model to cut cost.
gotchas.correct: Route by difficulty and confirm the quality impact on the same dataset and judge.

gotchas.trap: Raising concurrency to fix a slow step.
gotchas.correct: Find the bottleneck first. Concurrency raises throughput but doesn't shorten a slow sequential step.

gotchas.trap: Automatically retraining on every thumbs-down.
gotchas.correct: Review feedback, curate it into eval items, then fix and re-evaluate.

lessons.lab: Turn on `bottleneck_analysis` and `prompt_caching_prefixes` for an existing workflow, run `nat eval`, and use `gantt_chart.png` to name the slowest step. Make one change aimed at that step, re-run, and record the change in p95 latency and in AnswerAccuracy.

lessons.title: Serving agents with NIM containers on Kubernetes
lessons.summary: How NIM microservices package optimized inference as containers, and how to run them on Kubernetes with persistent caches, profiles, GPU-aware autoscaling and load balancing.

sections.heading: Why this domain matters
sections.body:
Deployment and Scaling is weighted **13%** on the NCP-AAI exam page, but the September 2025 study guide lists **5%**. Prepare to the higher figure. The study guide breaks the domain into five tasks:

- deploying and orchestrating multi-agent systems at production scale
- MLOps for CI/CD, monitoring and governance
- profiling under distributed load
- scaling with Docker and Kubernetes behind load balancers
- keeping costs down while staying highly available

This lesson covers the serving layer. The next two cover inference scaling, MLOps and cost.

sections.heading: NIM as the unit of deployment
sections.body:
An **NVIDIA NIM** for LLMs is a prebuilt inference microservice that ships as a container. The quickstart runs it with a published port (for example `-p 8000:8000`) and an **NGC API key**. Clients call an **OpenAI-compatible API** such as `/v1/chat/completions`.

The practical effect is that an agent written against an OpenAI-style client can usually switch to a self-hosted NIM by changing the base URL and model name. The agent logic stays the same.

NIM is part of **NVIDIA AI Enterprise**. The NIM catalog also includes vision-language, speech and retrieval microservices, so one agent system often runs several NIMs side by side.

sections.heading: Caches and profiles
sections.body:
- **Model cache.** Mount persistent storage at `NIM_CACHE_PATH`, which defaults to `/opt/nim/.cache`. Without a persistent mount, every container start downloads the model again. That causes slow cold starts and slow scale-out, and it adds egress cost.
- **Profiles.** A NIM picks an optimized *profile* (engine plus hardware configuration) for the GPUs it finds. Run `list-model-profiles` to see the profiles, and set `NIM_MODEL_PROFILE` to pin one. The preferred engine order has changed between NIM releases, so pin the profile explicitly when you need reproducible behavior.
- **Model-free image.** NIM 2.0.x adds a model-free image that takes a model path or a Hugging Face model.

sections.heading: Kubernetes, autoscaling and load balancing
sections.body:
On Kubernetes, NVIDIA provides the **NIM Operator** to manage NIM deployments declaratively. It handles the lifecycle of NIM microservices and their models, including model caching and autoscaling, so you don't hand-maintain `docker run` commands on each node.

Scaling signals matter. LLM serving is GPU-bound, so CPU utilization is often a poor autoscaling trigger. Export GPU telemetry with the **DCGM exporter** into **kube-prometheus** (NVIDIA's GPU telemetry guide, a study-guide reading), then scale on GPU and **request-queue** metrics.

Put several replicas behind a load balancer. Spread them across failure zones so that losing one node or zone does not take the agent down. For multi-agent systems, scale each agent service and each model endpoint on its own, because a planner, a retriever and a large reasoning model rarely have the same load profile.

keyPoints: NIM ships as a container with an OpenAI-compatible API and needs an NGC API key.
Mount NIM_CACHE_PATH (default /opt/nim/.cache) on persistent storage to avoid re-downloading the model.
Use list-model-profiles and NIM_MODEL_PROFILE to inspect and pin the engine/hardware profile.
Use the NIM Operator for Kubernetes lifecycle management.
Autoscale on GPU and queue metrics (DCGM exporter plus Prometheus), not CPU alone.

gotchas.trap: Autoscaling NIM pods on CPU utilization like a web service.
gotchas.correct: Scale on GPU utilization and request-queue depth exported via DCGM and Prometheus.

gotchas.trap: Running NIM pods with ephemeral storage only.
gotchas.correct: Mount a persistent volume at NIM_CACHE_PATH so restarts and new replicas reuse the cached model.

gotchas.trap: Rewriting the agent to call a proprietary NIM SDK.
gotchas.correct: NIM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so point the existing client at the NIM base URL.

lessons.lab: Run an LLM NIM locally with a host directory mounted at NIM_CACHE_PATH, list its profiles, then restart it and compare startup time with and without the cache mount. Point an OpenAI-style client at http://localhost:8000/v1 and send a chat completion.

lessons.title: Scaling inference and profiling under load
lessons.summary: Batching with Triton (now Dynamo-Triton), multi-node LLM serving with Dynamo, and using the NeMo Agent Toolkit profiler to find bottlenecks and size GPUs for agent workloads.

sections.heading: Batching on a single server
sections.body:
**Triton Inference Server**, now branded **NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton**, is the general multi-framework model server. Its batchers decide how requests share the GPU.

- The **dynamic batcher** combines individual requests on the server side. `max_queue_delay_microseconds` lets a batch wait briefly for more requests, then sends it as it is when the delay expires. The docs advise leaving `preferred_batch_size` unset in most cases. Queue policy sets `max_queue_size`, and priority levels are supported.
- The **sequence batcher** serves *stateful* models by routing every request in a sequence to the same model instance.
- For iterative (LLM-style) sequences, **in-flight batching** releases finished requests and reschedules in-flight ones on each iteration, which keeps the GPU busy.

sections.heading: Distributed LLM serving with Dynamo
sections.body:
**NVIDIA Dynamo** is an open-source distributed inference framework that sits above engines such as vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. It reached 1.0 GA in 2026, so do not describe it as experimental. Its headline features are:

- **Disaggregated prefill/decode serving.** The compute-heavy prompt (prefill) phase and the token-generation (decode) phase run on separate workers, so long prompts stop stalling generation for other users.
- **NIXL**, which transfers KV cache between workers.
- **KV-aware routing.** Requests go to workers that already hold the relevant KV cache, which avoids recomputing shared prefixes such as long agent system prompts.
- An SLO-driven **Planner** that adjusts GPU resources to meet service-level objectives.

sections.heading: Profiling agent workflows
sections.body:
The **NeMo Agent Toolkit (NAT)** profiler records per-invocation tokens, latency, and LLM and tool calls. `@track_function` instruments arbitrary code. It runs as part of `nat eval`, configured under the eval `profiler` settings. Useful options:

- `bottleneck_analysis` (nested-stack or simple-stack) finds which step dominates end-to-end latency.
- `concurrency_spike_analysis` with a `spike_threshold` flags moments when concurrent calls pile up.
- `prompt_caching_prefixes` finds shared prompt prefixes worth caching for KV reuse.
- `token_uniqueness_forecast` and `workflow_runtime_forecast` support capacity planning.

The outputs include `gantt_chart.png`, `workflow_profiling_report.txt`, `all_requests_profiler_traces.json` and `inference_optimization.json`. The last one reports latency, throughput and runtime with 90/95/99% confidence intervals. The **Sizing Calculator** (`nat sizing calc`) estimates the GPU cluster size needed for a target number of users and workflow runtime.

Use `--reps` for repeated runs and `eval.general.max_concurrency` to control load, so that comparisons reflect variance and not one lucky run.

sections.heading: Current status
sections.body: NVIDIA deprecated the NeMo Agent Toolkit in October 2026, with end of life at the end of 2026, and newer NeMo tools take over its roles. The exam blueprint (September 2025) still references the toolkit, under its earlier name Agent Intelligence Toolkit. Learn NAT for the exam, and check NVIDIA docs before you build anything new.

keyPoints: Triton (now Dynamo-Triton) dynamic batcher: max_queue_delay_microseconds trades a little latency for throughput; usually leave preferred_batch_size unset.
Sequence batcher keeps a stateful sequence on one model instance.
Dynamo: disaggregated prefill/decode, NIXL KV transfer, KV-aware routing, Planner.
NAT profiler: bottleneck and concurrency-spike analysis, prompt-prefix discovery, confidence intervals in inference_optimization.json.
nat sizing calc (the Sizing Calculator) estimates GPU requirements.

gotchas.trap: Hard-coding a large preferred_batch_size to "maximize throughput".
gotchas.correct: Enable dynamic batching with a small max queue delay and usually leave preferred_batch_size unset, as the Triton docs advise.

gotchas.trap: Round-robin load balancing for multi-turn LLM traffic with long shared prefixes.
gotchas.correct: Use KV-aware routing so requests land where the KV cache already exists.

gotchas.trap: Comparing two deployment configs on a single run.
gotchas.correct: Use repeated runs and confidence intervals before deciding.

lessons.title: MLOps, governance, cost and availability for agents
lessons.summary: Treat prompts, tools, models and configs as one versioned release, gate promotion on automated evaluation, roll out gradually, keep audit trails, and cut cost without losing availability.

sections.heading: What counts as a release
sections.body:
An agent's behavior depends on more than code: prompt templates, tool definitions and schemas, model identifiers (and the NIM profile), retrieval settings and workflow configuration. Version **all of these together**, so that any production behavior traces back to one release and a rollback restores all of it.

Avoid floating "latest" model references and hot-editing prompts in production. Both break reproducibility.

sections.heading: CI/CD with evaluation gates
sections.body:
Ordinary unit tests cannot catch a prompt change that quietly lowers answer quality. Add an **evaluation gate** to CI: run `nat eval --config_file=<workflow.yml>` against a fixed golden dataset with the same evaluators and judge as the baseline, and block promotion if scores regress.

NAT can also evaluate a running service with `--endpoint` (for a workflow started with `nat serve`), so the same check can run against a staging deployment.

Roll out with a **canary** (a small traffic slice, compared on live metrics) or **blue-green** (switch traffic between two full environments). Both give a fast rollback path.

sections.heading: Governance
sections.body:
Keep **audit logs** of agent decisions, tool calls and model and prompt versions, so you can explain and reconstruct any action. Combine them with access control on who can promote releases.

Governance belongs in the pipeline. A release that has no eval record or approval does not ship.

sections.heading: Cost without losing availability
sections.body:
Cost levers:

- **Right-size models per subtask.** Route easy queries or simple steps to smaller models and save the large model for hard reasoning.
- **Caching.** Use prompt and KV caching. The NAT profiler's `prompt_caching_prefixes` helps find shared prefixes.
- **Batching.** Raise GPU utilization with dynamic or in-flight batching.
- **Scale to zero in dev and test.** Not in production paths that must stay available.

Availability levers:

- multiple replicas across zones behind a load balancer
- autoscaling on queue depth
- persistent model caches so new replicas start fast
- graceful fallbacks when a dependency is down

Always check that a cost cut does not quietly remove the redundancy that keeps the service available.

keyPoints: Version prompts, tools, model IDs and configs together as one release.
Gate promotion on nat eval regression against a golden dataset.
Use canary or blue-green rollouts for limited blast radius and fast rollback.
Keep audit logs of decisions, tool calls and versions for governance.
Cut cost with model routing, caching, batching and dev scale-to-zero; keep cross-zone replicas for HA.

gotchas.trap: Pointing production at a floating "latest" model so improvements arrive automatically.
gotchas.correct: Pin model identifiers per release and promote changes through the eval gate.

gotchas.trap: Saving money by running production on a single large-GPU replica.
gotchas.correct: Keep redundant replicas across zones; save cost through routing, caching and batching instead.

gotchas.trap: Relying on unit tests alone for prompt changes.
gotchas.correct: Add automated quality evaluation on a fixed dataset to CI.

lessons.lab: Add a CI job that runs nat eval on a 20-item golden dataset and fails the build if the average evaluator score drops below the stored baseline. Then change a prompt so that quality drops, and confirm the gate blocks it.

lessons.title: Planning, decomposition, chain-of-thought and reflection
lessons.summary: How agents turn a goal into steps: the five planning families from the LLM-agent planning survey, chain-of-thought, ReAct vs ReWOO vs plan-and-execute, and reflection loops that let an agent correct itself.

sections.heading: Why planning is its own skill
sections.body: A single prompt-and-answer works for simple questions. Multi-step goals ("reconcile these invoices, flag mismatches, email the vendor") need the agent to **decide what to do next** many times, using results it did not have at the start. Planning is the part of the agent that chooses and orders those steps. Domain 5 asks you to pick a planning strategy for a scenario and to spot failure modes such as looping, drifting off-goal or committing to a broken plan.

sections.heading: The survey taxonomy (framework-neutral)
sections.body:
The survey *Understanding the Planning of LLM Agents* (arXiv:2402.02716) groups approaches into five families. They are useful vocabulary for scenario questions:

1. **Task decomposition**: split the goal into sub-goals, either all up front (decompose-first) or one at a time as you go (interleaved).
2. **Multi-plan selection**: generate several candidate plans or reasoning paths, then pick one by voting, scoring or search (tree-style exploration).
3. **External-module-aided planning**: hand the plan search to a classical planner or other tool and let the LLM translate in and out.
4. **Reflection and refinement**: critique the result or the failed step, then revise the plan.
5. **Memory-augmented planning**: retrieve past experiences or facts to inform the current plan.

Real agents mix these. A plan-and-execute agent is decomposition plus reflection; an agent that recalls how it solved a similar ticket last week adds memory augmentation.

sections.heading: Chain-of-thought and its limits
sections.body:
**Chain-of-thought (CoT)** prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, which improves multi-step arithmetic, logic and commonsense tasks on large models (arXiv:2201.11903). Variants include few-shot CoT (worked examples in the prompt), zero-shot CoT (an instruction to reason step by step) and self-consistency (sample several chains and take the majority answer, which is a form of multi-plan selection).

CoT on its own reasons **only over what is in the context**. It cannot fetch a fresh exchange rate or check a database, so for tasks that need external facts, combine reasoning with actions (tools or retrieval).

sections.heading: ReAct, ReWOO and plan-and-execute
sections.body:
- **ReAct** interleaves Thought, Action (tool call) and Observation. It adapts after every observation, which makes it robust when results are unpredictable, but it costs one LLM call per step and can loop.
- **ReWOO** (Reasoning WithOut Observation) plans **all tool calls up front** with placeholders, runs them, then a solver writes the answer. It needs fewer LLM calls and fewer tokens than ReAct, but it cannot easily adapt mid-way if an early tool returns something unexpected (arXiv:2305.18323).
- **Plan-and-execute** writes an explicit step list, executes steps (often with a cheaper model or tool calls) and **re-plans** when a step fails or new information changes the picture.

NVIDIA NeMo Agent Toolkit ships ready-made agent types including ReAct, ReWOO, Reasoning, Router, Tool Calling and Sequential/Parallel Executor agents, so these patterns are configuration choices rather than code you write from scratch.

sections.heading: Reflection and self-correction
sections.body:
**Reflection** adds a critique step: the agent (or a separate critic) inspects an answer, a failed tool call or a test result, writes down what went wrong, and tries again with that lesson in context. **Reflexion** (arXiv:2303.11366) stores these verbal self-reflections in an episodic memory buffer so later attempts improve without changing model weights.

Reflection works best with an **external signal**: a failing unit test, a schema validation error, a tool error code or a grader score. Asking a model to "double-check" with no new evidence often just restates the same mistake. Always cap reflection rounds so a stubborn task cannot loop forever.

sections.heading: Adapting from feedback and experience
sections.body: The study guide subtopic 5.5 asks you to adapt reasoning strategies from prior experience and feedback. In practice that means: log trajectories, keep lessons learned (reflections, successful plans) in long-term memory, retrieve them for similar tasks, and route structured user feedback into evaluation sets. Large models can also learn a task pattern from examples in the prompt (in-context learning) without retraining, which is why retrieved past examples can steer behaviour.

keyPoints: Survey families: task decomposition, multi-plan selection, external-module-aided planning, reflection and refinement, memory-augmented planning.
CoT improves multi-step reasoning but only over information already in context.
ReAct adapts per observation at the cost of more LLM calls; ReWOO plans all tool calls first and uses fewer calls.
Plan-and-execute keeps an explicit plan and re-plans when a step fails.
Reflection needs an external signal and a cap on the number of rounds.
NeMo Agent Toolkit provides ReAct, ReWOO, Reasoning, Router, Tool Calling and executor agent types.

gotchas.trap: Chain-of-thought lets the model look up facts it does not know.
gotchas.correct: CoT only reasons over the context. External facts need tools or retrieval.

gotchas.trap: ReWOO is always better than ReAct because it is cheaper.
gotchas.correct: ReWOO saves LLM calls when the plan is predictable; ReAct is better when each result changes what to do next.

gotchas.trap: Unlimited self-reflection eventually fixes any error.
gotchas.correct: Reflection without new evidence tends to repeat mistakes. Use an external signal and a round limit.

lessons.lab: Take a three-step task (look up a product's price, convert currency, compute a discount). Implement it twice in your framework of choice (or as NeMo Agent Toolkit `react_agent` and ReWOO workflows): once ReAct, once plan-first. Count LLM calls and tokens per run, then make the price lookup return an error and compare how each agent recovers. Add a reflection step that reads the tool error and retries at most twice.

lessons.title: Agent memory, context management and state persistence
lessons.summary: Short-term vs long-term memory (episodic, semantic, procedural), keeping the context window under control, and persisting orchestration state so multi-turn and long-running tasks survive restarts and interruptions.

sections.heading: Short-term memory: the context window
sections.body:
**Short-term (working) memory** is what the model sees on this call: system prompt, recent conversation turns, tool results and scratchpad reasoning. It is bounded by the context window and every token costs latency and money. Common management strategies:

- **Sliding window / trimming**: keep the last N turns or tokens; simple, but old facts silently disappear.
- **Summarization**: replace older turns with a running summary; keeps the gist, loses detail, and can drift if summaries are summarised repeatedly.
- **Selective retention**: pin critical facts (user ID, constraints, decisions) in a structured state block that is never trimmed.
- **Tool-result compaction**: store large tool outputs externally and keep only a reference or extract in context.

sections.heading: Long-term memory: three kinds
sections.body:
**Long-term memory** lives outside the model, in a database, vector store, graph store or object store, and is retrieved when relevant.

| Kind | Holds | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Episodic** | Past interactions and events | "Last month this customer's refund failed because the order was split." |
| **Semantic** | Facts and knowledge | User preferences, product facts, entity relationships (vector or graph store) |
| **Procedural** | How to do things | Learned workflows, successful plans, refined instructions |

Write policies matter as much as read policies: decide what is worth remembering, deduplicate, attach timestamps and provenance, and expire or correct stale facts. Scope memory per user or tenant so one user's memories never leak into another's session.

sections.heading: Memory in NeMo Agent Toolkit
sections.body:
NeMo Agent Toolkit includes an **Automatic Memory Wrapper** agent that adds memory retrieval and storage around another agent, plus pluggable memory and object-store backends. Redis memory support moved to a Redis-maintained `nemo-agent-toolkit-redis` package in the 1.9 line. For the exam, the point is architectural: memory is a component you configure and swap, separate from the reasoning agent.

*Current status:* NVIDIA deprecated NeMo Agent Toolkit in October 2026, with end of life at the end of 2026, in favour of NeMo Relay, NeMo Helix and NeMo Fabric. The exam guide (dated September 2025) still references the toolkit, so learn it as exam content.

sections.heading: State persistence for multi-turn tasks
sections.body:
Memory is about *knowledge*; **orchestration state** is about *where the task is*. A long-running agent needs to know which steps finished, what tools returned and what it is waiting for. The standard pattern is a stateful graph whose shared state is **checkpointed after each step and keyed by a thread or session ID**. That gives you:

- **Resume after crash or redeploy** from the last checkpoint instead of starting over (and re-running side effects).
- **Human-in-the-loop interrupts**: pause before an approval step, persist state, resume hours later when a person responds.
- **Isolation**: each conversation or job has its own thread ID, so concurrent users do not overwrite each other.
- **Debuggability**: replay or inspect state at any step.

Make side-effecting steps idempotent (or record completion in state) so a resumed run does not, for example, send the same email twice.

sections.heading: Choosing the right mechanism
sections.body:
- The user said something three turns ago and the agent forgot: a short-term context problem (trimming too aggressive, no pinned facts).
- The agent should know a returning user's preferences next week: long-term semantic memory with per-user scope.
- The agent should avoid repeating a failed approach on similar tasks: episodic or procedural memory (for example, stored reflections).
- A five-step job must survive a pod restart: checkpointed orchestration state, not a bigger context window.
- Stuffing everything into the prompt is rarely the answer: it raises cost and latency, and long noisy contexts can hurt accuracy.

keyPoints: Short-term memory is the context window; manage it with trimming, summarization, pinned state and compaction.
Long-term memory is external: episodic (events), semantic (facts), procedural (how-to).
Long-term memory needs write policies, provenance, expiry and per-user scoping.
Orchestration state is checkpointed per thread ID to support resume, interrupts and isolation.
Idempotent side effects keep resumed runs safe.
NeMo Agent Toolkit offers an Automatic Memory Wrapper agent and pluggable memory backends.

gotchas.trap: A larger context window removes the need for long-term memory.
gotchas.correct: Context is per call and costly; persistence across sessions and selective recall need external memory.

gotchas.trap: Memory and checkpointed state are the same thing.
gotchas.correct: Memory stores knowledge for recall; checkpoints store task progress so execution can resume.

gotchas.trap: One shared vector store for all users is fine if retrieval is accurate.
gotchas.correct: Scope memory by user or tenant to prevent cross-user leakage.

lessons.lab: Build a small chat agent with three layers: a sliding window of the last 6 turns, a pinned state block (user name, current goal), and a per-user vector store for facts the user asks it to remember. Then wrap a three-step task in a graph with a checkpointer keyed by thread ID; kill the process after step 2 and confirm it resumes at step 3 without repeating step 2's side effect.
