lessons.title: RAG pipelines for agents: retrieval, embeddings, reranking and vector databases
lessons.summary: How an agent grounds its answers in enterprise knowledge: ingestion, chunking, embeddings, approximate nearest neighbor search, hybrid retrieval, reranking, and where NVIDIA NeMo Retriever fits.

sections.heading: Why agents retrieve
sections.body:
A language model only knows what was in its training data and what is in its context window. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fixes both gaps at query time: the agent fetches relevant passages from an external store and puts them in the prompt, so answers can use **fresh or proprietary facts** and can **cite their sources**.

For an agent, retrieval is usually a **tool**, not a fixed pre-step. The agent decides when to search, rewrites the query, may search several times (multi-hop), and can choose among several knowledge tools: a vector index for documents, a SQL tool for the warehouse, a graph query for relationships, or a live API for data that changes by the minute.

The study guide lists this as Domain 6 subtopics 6.1 (retrieval pipelines: RAG, embedded search, hybrid approaches) and 6.2 (configure and optimize vector databases).

sections.heading: The two halves of a RAG pipeline
sections.body:
**Offline (ingestion) path**
1. *Extract* content from source documents: text, tables, charts, images.
2. *Chunk* the content into retrievable units, with a chosen size and overlap.
3. *Embed* each chunk with an embedding model into a dense vector.
4. *Index* the vectors plus metadata (source, section, date, access tags) in a vector database.

**Online (query) path**
1. Embed the query with the **same** embedding model.
2. Retrieve top-k candidates by vector similarity, optionally combined with keyword search and metadata filters.
3. Rerank the candidates and keep the best few.
4. Generate the answer from those passages, with citations.

A recurring exam theme: each stage has its own failure mode, so diagnose the stage before changing the model. If the right passage never reaches the prompt, no amount of prompt tuning or model swapping will fix the answer.

sections.heading: Chunking and embeddings
sections.body:
- **Chunk size** trades precision against context. Small chunks match narrowly but may lose surrounding meaning; large chunks carry context but dilute similarity and waste prompt tokens.
- **Overlap** keeps a sentence that straddles a boundary retrievable from either side.
- **Structure-aware chunking** (split on headings, keep tables whole, prepend the section title) usually beats fixed-width splitting for manuals and policies.
- **Embeddings must be consistent.** Vectors from different embedding models (or different versions) live in different spaces. If you change the embedding model, re-embed the whole corpus; never mix query vectors from one model with document vectors from another.

sections.heading: Vector databases and ANN indexes
sections.body:
Exact (flat) search compares the query with every vector, which is accurate but scales linearly. Production systems use **approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)** indexes:

- **HNSW** (hierarchical navigable small world graphs): fast, high recall, more memory.
- **IVF** (inverted file): clusters vectors and only searches the nearest clusters.

Both expose knobs that trade recall for latency. Milvus, the vector database NeMo Retriever extraction ingests into, supports GPU-accelerated indexing and search (for example GPU_CAGRA and GPU_IVF_* indexes) built on NVIDIA RAPIDS libraries such as cuVS.

Store **metadata** next to each vector and filter on it (tenant, department, document type, date). Filtering by the user's entitlements at retrieval time is how you stop an agent from surfacing documents the user should not see; a system-prompt instruction is not an access control.

sections.heading: Hybrid search and reranking
sections.body:
- **Dense retrieval** captures meaning and paraphrase but can miss exact tokens such as part numbers, error codes or names.
- **Sparse/keyword retrieval (for example BM25)** nails exact terms but misses paraphrase.
- **Hybrid search** runs both and fuses the results, which is the usual fix when queries mix natural language with identifiers.

**Reranking** is a second stage. The first stage cheaply pulls a generous candidate set (for example top 50). A reranker, typically a cross-encoder that reads the query and each passage *together*, scores every pair and reorders them; you keep the top few. It improves precision, but it can only reorder what the first stage returned, so it does not fix recall.

sections.heading: Where NVIDIA NeMo Retriever fits
sections.body:
**NeMo Retriever** is a family of NIM microservices for the RAG pipeline:

- **Extraction** (also called NVIDIA Ingest or **nv-ingest**) pulls text, tables, charts and images out of documents. It runs through `nv-ingest-cli` or a Python API and ingests into Milvus. For scanned pages or complex layouts it can use **nemoretriever-parse**, and it calls NIM services for image OCR and object detection.
- **Text Embedding NIM** turns chunks and queries into vectors.
- **Text Reranking NIM** scores query-passage pairs to reorder candidates.

The embedding and reranking NIMs expose OpenAI-compatible and gRPC APIs. NVIDIA also publishes a **Build a RAG Pipeline** blueprint on build.nvidia.com as a reference workflow that wires these pieces together.

> **Current status:** model names and versions in the NeMo Retriever catalog change often. Learn the roles (extract, embed, rerank) rather than specific model names.

keyPoints: RAG supplies fresh, proprietary and citable facts at query time; for agents, retrieval is usually a tool the agent chooses to call.
Diagnose by stage: extraction, chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, generation.
Queries and documents must be embedded with the same model; changing models means re-embedding the corpus.
ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF) trade a little recall for large latency gains; Milvus can GPU-accelerate them with cuVS.
Hybrid (keyword plus dense) search fixes missed identifiers; reranking fixes ordering but not recall.
NeMo Retriever = NIM microservices for extraction (nv-ingest), embedding and reranking.

gotchas.trap: Adding a reranker will fix answers when the correct passage never appears in the top-k.
gotchas.correct: A reranker only reorders candidates. Fix recall first: hybrid search, better chunking, a larger first-stage k, or query rewriting.

gotchas.trap: Telling the model in the system prompt not to reveal restricted documents is enough.
gotchas.correct: Enforce entitlements with metadata filters at retrieval time so restricted chunks never reach the prompt.

gotchas.trap: Upgrading the embedding model for queries only is a safe incremental rollout.
gotchas.correct: Vectors from different models are not comparable; re-embed the corpus (or run a parallel index) before switching queries.

lessons.lab: Take 20 internal-style documents that include a table and a few part numbers. Build two indexes: fixed 512-token chunks with dense-only retrieval, and structure-aware chunks with hybrid retrieval plus a reranker. Write 15 test questions (some with exact identifiers) and record, for each index, whether the correct passage appears in the top 5. Note which failures came from recall and which from ordering.

lessons.title: Knowledge graphs, GraphRAG and structured knowledge for agents
lessons.summary: When similarity search is the wrong tool: relational and multi-hop questions, knowledge graphs and GraphRAG, and giving agents safe access to structured data such as SQL warehouses and live APIs.

sections.heading: Where vector RAG runs out
sections.body:
Vector search answers "find passages that look like this question". It struggles when the answer depends on **relationships** spread across many documents:

- *Multi-hop*: "Which suppliers of parts used in product X are located in region Y?" needs product -> parts -> suppliers -> locations.
- *Aggregation and global questions*: "What are the main themes across all incident reports this year?" is not answered by any single chunk.
- *Exact structured facts*: "What was Q3 revenue by region?" lives in a table, not in prose.

Raising top-k or chunk size rarely fixes these; it just adds noise. The fix is to pick a knowledge representation that matches the question.

sections.heading: Knowledge graphs
sections.body:
A **knowledge graph** stores entities as nodes and relationships as typed edges (for example `Part -SUPPLIED_BY-> Supplier -LOCATED_IN-> Region`). An agent can answer relational questions by **traversing** edges or by issuing a graph query, and the path itself is an explanation of the answer.

Knowledge graphs are built by extracting entities and relations from documents (often with an LLM), by mapping existing structured data, or both. The study guide lists integrating knowledge graphs for relational reasoning under Domain 1 (1.7), so expect graph questions to show up as architecture choices as well.

sections.heading: GraphRAG
sections.body:
**GraphRAG** combines the two approaches. During indexing, an LLM extracts an entity-relationship graph from the corpus, the graph is partitioned into communities, and summaries are generated for those communities. At query time the system can answer:

- **Local** questions by starting from the entities in the query and pulling in their neighborhood plus the source passages.
- **Global** questions ("what are the main themes?") by combining community summaries, which plain vector RAG handles poorly.

The trade-off is cost and complexity: graph extraction is LLM-heavy at index time and must be refreshed as documents change.

sections.heading: Structured data: give the agent a query tool
sections.body:
For tables, warehouses and operational systems, the usual pattern is not to embed rows but to give the agent a **tool**:

- A **text-to-SQL** or parameterized-query tool against a read-only replica or view, with the schema (tables, columns, meanings) provided as context.
- A **live API** tool for data that changes faster than any index can be refreshed (prices, inventory, ticket status).

Guard these tools the way you guard any tool: least-privilege credentials, read-only access where possible, validated arguments, row limits and timeouts. Return results with their provenance so the agent can cite them.

A strong agent routes each question: documents to the retriever, relationships to the graph, numbers to SQL, and live state to the API. Hybrid pipelines often combine several in one answer.

keyPoints: Use vector RAG for "find similar passages"; use a graph for relationships and multi-hop questions.
GraphRAG builds an entity graph plus community summaries at index time, which helps both local and global (whole-corpus) questions.
For tabular facts, prefer a guarded SQL or API tool over embedding rows.
Live data belongs behind a tool call, not in an index that is refreshed on a schedule.
Agents should route each question to the representation that fits it, and cite provenance.

gotchas.trap: A multi-hop relational question fails, so increase top-k and chunk size.
gotchas.correct: Model the relationships explicitly (knowledge graph or GraphRAG) so the agent can traverse them.

gotchas.trap: Embed every warehouse row as a chunk so the agent can "search" revenue figures.
gotchas.correct: Expose a read-only, schema-aware query tool; similarity search cannot reliably aggregate or filter numbers.

lessons.lab: Sketch a small graph (about 30 nodes) of products, parts, suppliers and regions. Write three questions: one a single document can answer, one multi-hop, and one aggregate. For each, decide which tool an agent should use (vector search, graph traversal, or SQL) and write the query or traversal it would run.

lessons.title: Data handling for agents: ETL, multimodal content, quality and freshness
lessons.summary: Turning messy enterprise sources into trustworthy agent knowledge: ETL for structured, unstructured and multimodal data, data quality checks and preprocessing, and keeping indexes fresh.

sections.heading: ETL for agent knowledge
sections.body:
The study guide adds two subtopics that are easy to overlook: **6.3 build ETL pipelines to integrate enterprise or client data sources** and **6.4 conduct data quality checks, augmentation and preprocessing**.

A knowledge ETL pipeline for an agent typically:
1. **Extracts** from sources: file shares, wikis, ticketing systems, databases, object storage.
2. **Transforms**: parse formats, extract tables and images, clean and normalize text, deduplicate, chunk, attach metadata (source URL, owner, timestamps, access tags), and embed.
3. **Loads** into the right stores: a vector database, a graph, a search index, or a warehouse.

Treat it like any production data pipeline: idempotent steps, versioned configuration, monitoring, and the ability to reprocess when the chunking strategy or embedding model changes.

sections.heading: Structured, unstructured and multimodal data
sections.body:
- **Structured** (tables, rows, JSON records): keep the structure. Load into a queryable store and expose it via a tool; if tables must be retrieved as text, serialize them so the header and units stay with the values.
- **Unstructured** (prose documents, emails, transcripts): extract text cleanly, preserve headings, and chunk along the document's structure.
- **Semi-structured and multimodal** (PDFs with tables, charts, scanned pages, diagrams, images): naive text extraction drops or scrambles tables and ignores charts. NeMo Retriever extraction (nv-ingest) is built for this: it pulls text, tables, charts and images separately, and uses nemoretriever-parse for scanned or complex layouts along with OCR and object-detection NIMs. Images and charts can then be made retrievable, for example through generated descriptions or multimodal embeddings (NIM's catalog includes vision-language models and NV-CLIP), while keeping a link back to the source page.

sections.heading: Data quality checks and preprocessing
sections.body:
Retrieval quality is bounded by corpus quality. Common checks:

- **Deduplication** (exact and near-duplicate) so the same paragraph does not fill every top-k slot.
- **Boilerplate removal**: navigation menus, legal footers, repeated headers.
- **Encoding and language normalization**, broken characters, empty or tiny chunks.
- **Metadata completeness**: every chunk has source, date and access tags; missing tags should fail the load rather than default to "public".
- **PII handling** according to policy before content enters a shared index.
- **Augmentation** where useful: generated titles or summaries per chunk, synonyms, or synthetic question-answer pairs used to evaluate retrieval.

Track quality with a fixed set of test queries whose correct sources are known, and rerun it after every pipeline change.

sections.heading: Freshness
sections.body:
Stale knowledge produces confident wrong answers. Match the refresh method to how fast the data changes:

- **Slow-changing documents**: scheduled **incremental** indexing that upserts changed documents and deletes removed ones, keyed by a stable document ID and modification timestamp. Full re-indexing is reserved for chunking or embedding-model changes.
- **Frequently changing records**: **change data capture (CDC)** or event-driven updates from the source system.
- **Real-time state** (prices, stock, order status): do not index it at all; give the agent a live query tool.

Store timestamps in metadata so the agent can prefer recent sources, filter by date, and tell the user how current an answer is.

keyPoints: Domain 6 includes ETL (6.3) and data quality, augmentation and preprocessing (6.4), not just retrieval.
Keep structure: tables and records belong in queryable stores or carefully serialized chunks.
Multimodal documents need extraction that handles tables, charts, images and scans (for example nv-ingest).
Deduplicate, strip boilerplate, enforce metadata and handle PII before indexing.
Freshness: incremental upserts and deletes, CDC for fast-changing sources, live tools for real-time data.

gotchas.trap: Run a nightly full re-index to keep a large corpus fresh.
gotchas.correct: Use incremental upserts and deletes keyed by document ID and timestamp; reserve full rebuilds for embedding or chunking changes.

gotchas.trap: Flatten PDFs to plain text and chunk every 512 tokens.
gotchas.correct: Use layout-aware extraction that keeps tables, charts and images, and chunk along document structure.

gotchas.trap: Missing access tags can default to public so ingestion does not fail.
gotchas.correct: Fail closed: a chunk without entitlement metadata should not be loaded into a shared index.

lessons.title: The NVIDIA inference stack: NIM, TensorRT-LLM, Triton and Dynamo
lessons.summary: Which NVIDIA serving component to use for which job, how they layer on top of each other, and the batching and caching settings that cut latency.

sections.heading: Four layers, four jobs
sections.body:
Exam scenarios often name several NVIDIA products and ask which one fixes the problem. Each component works at a different layer:

| Component | Layer | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| **TensorRT-LLM** | Engine and library | You need lower LLM latency and memory use: optimized kernels, quantization (FP8/FP4/INT4), in-flight batching, paged KV cache |
| **Triton Inference Server** (now **NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton**) | General model server | You serve many models or frameworks behind one server: multi-framework backends, dynamic batching, ensembles |
| **Dynamo** | Distributed LLM serving | One model has to span many GPUs or nodes: disaggregated prefill/decode, KV-aware routing, KV transfer via NIXL, a Planner |
| **NIM** | Packaged microservice | You want a prebuilt, optimized model container with an OpenAI-compatible API, ready quickly |

These are layers, not rivals. A NIM container picks an engine profile (TensorRT-LLM among them) for you. Dynamo sits above engines such as vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM.

sections.heading: NIM in practice
sections.body:
- A NIM runs as a container and exposes an **OpenAI-compatible API**, for example `/v1/chat/completions`. Pulling it requires an NGC API key.
- **Mount a model cache** at `NIM_CACHE_PATH` (default `/opt/nim/.cache`). Without the mount, the model downloads again every time the container starts.
- **Profiles** choose the engine and hardware configuration automatically. `list-model-profiles` shows the options and `NIM_MODEL_PROFILE` pins one. The default engine preference has changed between NIM releases, so check the docs for your version rather than assuming one.
- On Kubernetes, the **NIM Operator** manages NIM deployments. NIM is part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise.
- Multimodal NIMs exist too: vision language models, speech (Riva) and NV-CLIP. For document ingestion, **NeMo Retriever** NIMs handle extraction, embedding and reranking.

sections.heading: Triton batching knobs
sections.body:
- The **dynamic batcher** combines separate requests on the server so the GPU processes them together. `max_queue_delay_microseconds` lets a batch wait briefly for more requests. When the delay expires, the batch goes as it is. The docs recommend leaving `preferred_batch_size` unset in most cases.
- The **sequence batcher** is for **stateful** models. It routes every request in a sequence to the same model instance.
- For iterative (LLM-style) sequences, **in-flight batching** releases finished requests and schedules waiting ones at each iteration, so a long generation doesn't hold up short ones.
- **Ensembles** chain models, such as preprocess, model and postprocess, inside the server without extra network round-trips.

sections.heading: Naming you will see
sections.body: The study guide still says "Triton Inference Server". NVIDIA has since rebranded it **NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton** as part of the Dynamo platform. Either name may appear in a question, and both mean the same server. Dynamo has also reached general availability, so treat it as a production option, not an experiment.

keyPoints: TensorRT-LLM optimizes the engine. Triton (Dynamo-Triton) serves models. Dynamo spreads one LLM across GPUs and nodes. NIM packages all of it as an API.
NIM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so existing OpenAI-style clients only need a new base URL.
Mount NIM_CACHE_PATH so the model isn't downloaded again on every container start.
Use the dynamic batcher for stateless throughput and the sequence batcher for stateful models.
Disaggregated prefill/decode and KV-aware routing are Dynamo features.

gotchas.trap: Choosing TensorRT-LLM when the team just needs a working endpoint this week.
gotchas.correct: Use NIM. It already packages an optimized engine behind an OpenAI-compatible API. Use TensorRT-LLM directly only when you need custom engine control.

gotchas.trap: Setting preferred_batch_size first to tune Triton's dynamic batcher.
gotchas.correct: Start by enabling the dynamic batcher with a small max_queue_delay_microseconds. The docs say preferred_batch_size should usually stay unset.

gotchas.trap: Using the dynamic batcher for a model that keeps state across requests.
gotchas.correct: Stateful models need the sequence batcher, which sends every request in a sequence to the same instance.

lessons.lab: Pull an LLM NIM with an NGC key. Run it once without a cache volume and once with NIM_CACHE_PATH mounted, and compare startup times. Run list-model-profiles, then call /v1/chat/completions with an OpenAI client pointed at the container.

lessons.title: Agent layer: NeMo Agent Toolkit, NeMo Guardrails and Blueprints
lessons.summary: How NVIDIA's agent-side tools fit on top of NIM: NAT for building, evaluating and profiling workflows across frameworks, Guardrails for safety rails, and Blueprints as reference starting points.

sections.heading: How the pieces stack
sections.body:
A typical NVIDIA agent stack looks like this, from top to bottom:

1. **Blueprint**: a reference workflow you start from and customize, such as AI-Q for deep research or a RAG pipeline.
2. **NeMo Agent Toolkit (NAT)**: wires agents, tools and LLMs together in YAML, and evaluates and profiles the workflow.
3. **NeMo Guardrails**: programmable rails around the LLM's input, retrieval, dialog, tool execution and output.
4. **NIM / NeMo Retriever**: the model, embedding and reranking endpoints.
5. **TensorRT-LLM, Triton (Dynamo-Triton), Dynamo**: the engines and servers underneath.

sections.heading: NeMo Agent Toolkit (NAT)
sections.body:
- Install with the pip package `nvidia-nat` and run the `nat` CLI. It is Apache-2.0 licensed. Earlier names were AgentIQ and **Agent Intelligence Toolkit** (`aiqtoolkit`, CLI `aiq`). The study guide uses the older name.
- NAT is **framework-agnostic**. Plugins cover LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, AutoGen, Semantic Kernel and others, so you can profile a mixed-framework workflow as one system.
- Tools are registered as Functions or Function Groups and wired together in a YAML workflow config. Built-in agent types include ReAct, ReWOO, Reasoning, Router and Tool Calling.
- NAT includes an MCP client and server and an A2A client and server.
- `nat eval --config_file=...` runs evaluators such as `ragas`, `trajectory` and `tunable_rag_evaluator` against a dataset. `--reps` repeats runs so you can measure variance.
- The **profiler** records tokens, latency and LLM/tool calls for every invocation. It does bottleneck analysis, finds shared prompt prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and produces a Gantt chart. `nat serve` exposes the workflow as an API server, and NAT also ships a built-in chat UI.

> **Current status:** NVIDIA deprecated NAT in October 2026 and named successor tools. The exam guide still tests NAT, so learn it as described here and check the GitHub README for what replaces it in new projects.

sections.heading: NeMo Guardrails
sections.body:
- There are five **rail types**: **input** (screen user messages, e.g. jailbreak detection or PII masking), **retrieval** (filter retrieved chunks, which helps against indirect prompt injection), **dialog** (keep the conversation on allowed topics and flows), **execution** (check tool and action calls) and **output** (content safety and PII on responses).
- Flows are written in **Colang**. `config.yml` sets models, prompts, rails and tracing, and custom actions are Python functions.
- Built-in `self check input` and `self check output` flows use an LLM with prompts kept in `prompts.yml`. For stronger checks, NVIDIA offers dedicated **NemoGuard NIMs** for content safety, topic control and jailbreak detection.
- `nemoguardrails server` runs the rails as a service with a `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint. Guardrails also integrates with LangChain and LangGraph.

sections.heading: Blueprints
sections.body: NVIDIA Blueprints (formerly "NIM Agent Blueprints") are **reference workflows**: sample code, deployment configs and documentation that combine NIM, NeMo and partner tools for one use case. Examples include the AI-Q research agent, a RAG pipeline, video search and summarization, and voice agents. The catalog changes often. The exam tests the concept: start from a blueprint and customize it rather than building from scratch.

keyPoints: NAT connects, evaluates and profiles agent workflows across frameworks. It doesn't replace LangGraph or CrewAI.
nat eval scores a workflow against a dataset. The profiler finds latency and token bottlenecks.
The five Guardrails rail types are input, retrieval, dialog, execution and output.
Retrieval rails defend against indirect prompt injection hidden in retrieved documents.
Blueprints are reference workflows you customize, not managed products.

gotchas.trap: Rewriting a mixed LangGraph + LlamaIndex agent in a single framework just so you can profile it.
gotchas.correct: NAT plugins wrap several frameworks, so the profiler and evaluators work on the workflow as it is.

gotchas.trap: Relying only on an input rail to stop prompt injection.
gotchas.correct: Injected instructions can arrive in retrieved content and tool results. Layer retrieval, execution and output rails as well.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the exam name "Agent Intelligence Toolkit" is a different product.
gotchas.correct: It is an earlier name of the NeMo Agent Toolkit (aiqtoolkit, then nvidia-nat).

lessons.lab: Install nvidia-nat and run an example ReAct workflow with nat run. Add a small JSON dataset and run nat eval with the trajectory evaluator, then read the profiler output in the output directory. Separately, create a Guardrails config.yml with self check input and self check output and run nemoguardrails server.

lessons.title: Observability and Tracing for Agent Runs
lessons.summary: How to instrument an agent so every run can be reconstructed: spans for LLM, tool and retrieval steps, the reliability metrics a dashboard should show, and how NeMo Agent Toolkit exports telemetry.

sections.heading: Why agents need traces, not just logs
sections.body:
A single user request to an agent can fan out into many LLM calls, tool calls and retrievals, and the path changes from run to run. A flat application log rarely tells you *which* step went wrong. The fix is **distributed tracing**: model each run as a **trace** made of nested **spans**, one per step.

For each span, record at least:
- the step type (LLM call, tool call, retrieval, guardrail check) and its name
- inputs and outputs (redacted where they contain sensitive data)
- latency, token counts and estimated cost
- errors, retries and status codes

With that structure you can open one failed run and see that, for example, the retriever returned irrelevant chunks, the LLM answered anyway, and the output looked confident.

sections.heading: Reliability metrics for a monitoring dashboard
sections.body:
The study guide asks you to *define monitoring dashboards and reliability metrics*. For agents, pure infrastructure metrics are not enough. A useful dashboard combines:

| Metric | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Task success rate | Is the agent completing the job end to end? |
| Tool-error rate | Are integrations failing (timeouts, auth, bad arguments)? |
| p95 / p99 latency | Tail experience, not just the average |
| Tokens and cost per request | Runaway loops and prompt bloat |
| Groundedness / answer accuracy | Are answers supported by the retrieved context? |
| Escalation rate | How often humans have to take over |

Track these over time and per version so that a regression shows up as a step change after a release.

sections.heading: Telemetry in NeMo Agent Toolkit
sections.body:
NeMo Agent Toolkit (NAT) includes an **Observe Workflows** capability built on **OpenTelemetry**-based telemetry exporters, with native **LangSmith** integration; the project also credits Phoenix and Weave as observability integrations. Because exporters are standard OpenTelemetry, traces can go to whichever backend your organization already runs, instead of a bespoke log format.

NAT's **profiler** complements tracing: it collects per-invocation tokens, latency, and LLM and tool calls, and `@track_function` instruments arbitrary Python functions. Its outputs include `all_requests_profiler_traces.json`, a `gantt_chart.png` and bottleneck analysis, which help you find the slow step in a multi-step workflow.

> **Current status:** NVIDIA deprecated NAT in October 2026 in favour of newer NeMo components. The exam study guide still teaches NAT (and its earlier names), so learn it as exam content.

sections.heading: Propagating trace context across protocols
sections.body: Agents often call tools on other servers. If the trace breaks at every hop, you lose the end-to-end picture. The MCP specification reserves the W3C trace-context keys `traceparent`, `tracestate` and `baggage` in a request's `_meta` field so a client can pass its trace context to an MCP server. Use the same idea for any internal service: forward the trace ID on every call so spans from different processes join one trace.

keyPoints: Model each agent run as a trace with one span per LLM call, tool call and retrieval.
Record latency, tokens, cost and errors on every span so you can find the failing or slow step.
Agent dashboards need task success, tool-error rate, tail latency, groundedness and escalation rate, not just CPU and memory.
NAT's Observe Workflows uses OpenTelemetry-based exporters and integrates natively with LangSmith.
MCP reserves traceparent, tracestate and baggage in _meta for W3C trace-context propagation.

gotchas.trap: Average latency looks fine, so users must be happy.
gotchas.correct: Agent latency has long tails from loops and retries; watch p95/p99 and per-step spans.

gotchas.trap: Logging only the final answer is enough to debug a bad response.
gotchas.correct: You need the intermediate steps (retrieved context, tool inputs and outputs) to find the root cause.

gotchas.trap: Each microservice can start its own trace.
gotchas.correct: Propagate trace context (for example via W3C traceparent) so all hops join one end-to-end trace.

lessons.lab: Take a small tool-calling agent and wrap each LLM call, tool call and retrieval in an OpenTelemetry span with attributes for latency, token count and error status. Send the traces to any OTel-compatible backend, run ten queries including one that forces a tool timeout, and find the failed span from the trace view alone.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting and Maintaining Live Agents
lessons.summary: A root-cause workflow for hallucinations and tool failures, plus how to keep a deployed agent healthy with version-against-version benchmarks, drift monitoring and controlled updates.

sections.heading: Diagnosing hallucinations
sections.body:
When a RAG-backed agent gives a confident wrong answer, work from the evidence in the trace rather than immediately changing the model:

1. **Check retrieval first.** Were the right documents retrieved? Low context relevance means the problem is upstream (chunking, embeddings, filters, stale index), and no prompt change will fix it.
2. **Then check grounding.** If the right context was present, did the answer stick to it? Low groundedness points at the prompt, the model, or missing instructions to cite or abstain.
3. **Check tool outputs.** A tool that silently returned an empty or error payload can lead the model to invent data.

NAT's `ragas` evaluator exposes metrics that map neatly onto this split: **ContextRelevance** (retrieval), **ResponseGroundedness** (grounding) and **AnswerAccuracy** (end result), each scored from 0 to 1.

sections.heading: Diagnosing tool failures
sections.body:
Tool failures show up as error spans, retries, or the model looping on the same call. Separate the causes:
- **Transient** faults (timeouts, rate limits, 5xx): handle with bounded retries with backoff and a circuit breaker so you stop hammering a failing dependency.
- **Persistent** faults (auth expired, schema changed, endpoint removed): retries only add latency and cost; alert and fail gracefully.
- **Model-side** faults (wrong tool chosen, malformed arguments): fix tool descriptions and schemas, and validate arguments before execution.

A rising tool-error rate on the dashboard right after an upstream API release is a classic signal of the persistent kind.

sections.heading: Benchmark every release against the previous one
sections.body:
The study guide asks you to *continuously benchmark deployed agents against prior versions*. Keep a fixed golden dataset and run the same evaluation, with the same judge, against the current and candidate versions. With NAT this is `nat eval --config_file=<workflow.yml>`; use `--reps=N` to measure run-to-run variance before you conclude one version is better, and `--endpoint` to evaluate a workflow already running under `nat serve`. Each run writes `config_effective.yml` alongside the evaluator outputs, so you can tell exactly which configuration produced which score.

Version prompts, tool definitions, model IDs and configuration **together**: an agent's behaviour depends on all of them, so changing any one is a release.

sections.heading: Drift, updates and uptime
sections.body:
Live agents degrade even when nobody changes the code: source documents go stale, user questions shift, and upstream models or APIs change. Monitor input distributions and data-quality signals, and re-run evaluations on fresh samples of production traffic. Feed reviewed failures and structured user feedback back into the evaluation set (a data flywheel) so the benchmark keeps reflecting reality.

Roll out updates gradually (canary or blue-green), compare live metrics between old and new, and keep the previous version ready for a fast rollback. That is how you deliver the study guide's goal of continuous uptime, transparency and trust.

keyPoints: Debug hallucinations retrieval-first: check context relevance, then groundedness, then tool outputs.
Retry transient tool faults with backoff and a circuit breaker; alert on persistent ones instead of retrying.
Benchmark new versions against prior ones on a fixed dataset with the same judge, and use repeated runs to measure variance.
Version prompts, tools, model IDs and configs together; any change is a release.
Monitor drift, recycle production failures into the eval set, and use canary or blue-green rollouts with fast rollback.

gotchas.trap: Hallucinations mean you need a bigger model.
gotchas.correct: Most RAG hallucinations trace back to poor retrieval; check context relevance first.

gotchas.trap: One better eval run proves the new version is better.
gotchas.correct: LLM outputs vary between runs; repeat runs (for example nat eval --reps) before comparing.

gotchas.trap: Retry every tool error a few more times.
gotchas.correct: Retries only help transient faults; persistent faults like expired credentials need alerts and graceful failure.

lessons.title: Layered Safety with NeMo Guardrails
lessons.summary: How to build defence in depth around an agent: the five NeMo Guardrails rail types, the NVIDIA safety models that plug into them, and where escalation to a human fits.

sections.heading: Why one filter is never enough
sections.body:
An agent takes untrusted input, retrieves untrusted documents, calls tools that change things, and returns generated text. A single system-prompt instruction such as "never reveal customer data" protects none of these reliably. The model can be talked out of it, and the instruction does nothing about retrieved or tool content.

A **layered safety framework** puts independent checks at every boundary, so a miss in one layer can be caught by the next. Each layer is cheap to reason about, can be tested on its own, and leaves a record for audit.

sections.heading: The five rail types
sections.body:
NeMo Guardrails organises programmable checks into five rail types:

| Rail | Runs on | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Input** | the user message | jailbreak and injection detection, PII masking, rejecting off-policy requests |
| **Dialog** | the conversation flow | keeping the bot on approved topics, scripted responses, routing |
| **Retrieval** | retrieved chunks in RAG | dropping or masking chunks, which helps against *indirect* prompt injection |
| **Execution** | tool / action calls | validating inputs and outputs of actions before and after they run |
| **Output** | the generated answer | content safety, PII leakage, fact or policy checks |

Flows are written in **Colang**. A `config.yml` file declares the models, prompts, active rails and tracing, and custom actions are plain Python functions. The built-in `self check input` and `self check output` flows ask an LLM to judge a message against a policy prompt kept in `prompts.yml`.

sections.heading: Plugging in NVIDIA safety models
sections.body:
Self-check prompts are a start, but they rely on an LLM judging its own traffic. Dedicated safety models add purpose-built checks as separate rails. The Guardrails docs list integrations including:

- **Jailbreak protection**: self-check, heuristics, and the **NemoGuard Jailbreak Detection NIM**.
- **Content safety**: the **NemoGuard Content Safety** model (Llama 3.1 based), with newer safety-guard models appearing in the NIM catalog.
- **Topic control**: the **NemoGuard Topic Control NIM**, which keeps a bot within its allowed scope.
- **PII detection**: integrations such as Presidio and NVIDIA GLiNER-PII.

Model names in this family change often, so learn the *role* each one plays (jailbreak, content safety, topic, PII) rather than a version string.

sections.heading: Serving and escalation
sections.body:
Guardrails can run inside your Python app, in LangChain or LangGraph, or as a server (`nemoguardrails server --config ./config`) that exposes an OpenAI-style `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint. The server option lets several apps share one policy configuration.

Rails decide whether to allow, block, rewrite or escalate. **Escalation protocols** matter most for high-risk or ambiguous cases. When a rail flags a request it can't settle, or the agent is about to take an irreversible action, route it to a human reviewer instead of silently failing or silently proceeding.

keyPoints: Five rail types: input, dialog, retrieval, execution, output.
Colang defines flows; config.yml declares models, rails and tracing; prompts.yml holds self-check prompts; actions are Python.
Dedicated NemoGuard NIMs cover jailbreak detection, content safety and topic control. Presidio and GLiNER-PII cover PII.
Retrieval rails are the layer aimed at indirect prompt injection from documents.
Escalate to a human for ambiguous or irreversible cases. Don't silently block or silently proceed.

gotchas.trap: A strong system prompt is enough to keep the agent safe.
gotchas.correct: Prompts can be overridden by jailbreaks and don't cover retrieved or tool content. Use independent rails at each boundary.

gotchas.trap: Input rails alone stop prompt injection.
gotchas.correct: Injected instructions often arrive in retrieved documents or tool output. Add retrieval and execution rails too.

gotchas.trap: Memorise the exact safety-model version names.
gotchas.correct: The names change often. Know each model's role: jailbreak, content safety, topic control, PII.

lessons.lab: Create a NeMo Guardrails config with `self check input` and `self check output` enabled and policy prompts in prompts.yml. Run it with `nemoguardrails server --config ./config`, then send a benign request, a jailbreak attempt, and a request that would leak an email address. Note which rail fired for each one.

lessons.title: Injection, Privacy, Bias, Audit and Regulation
lessons.summary: The policy side of agent safety: treating tool and retrieved content as untrusted, least privilege and approval gates, privacy controls, bias and toxicity mitigation, audit trails, and principle-level regulatory compliance.

sections.heading: Prompt injection: everything external is untrusted
sections.body:
**Direct injection** comes from the user ("ignore your instructions..."). **Indirect injection** hides instructions in content the agent reads: a web page, an email, a retrieved chunk, or a tool result. An agent that obeys such text can leak data or misuse tools.

Defences work together:
- Treat retrieved content and tool output as **data, never instructions**. Filter it with retrieval rails.
- Give each tool **least privilege**: read-only where possible, narrowly scoped credentials, allow-listed destinations.
- Require **human approval** for side-effecting or irreversible actions such as payments, deletions and external emails.
- Validate tool calls with execution rails before they run.

MCP takes the same stance: tool annotations and descriptions from a server are untrusted unless the server itself is trusted.

sections.heading: Privacy and enterprise policy
sections.body:
Privacy preservation means minimising what sensitive data enters and leaves the system:
- Detect and **mask PII** on input before it reaches the model or logs, and on output before it reaches the user.
- Keep only the data the task needs, and redact traces and logs that hold user content.
- Encode enterprise policy (approved topics, data-handling rules) as rails, so it's enforced the same way every time and can be tested.

sections.heading: Bias and toxicity
sections.body:
Bias and toxicity are mitigated at several levels:
- **Measure**: evaluate outputs across demographic or user slices with a fixed test set, and track toxicity and refusal rates per slice, not just overall.
- **Filter**: use content-safety output rails to block toxic or harmful generations.
- **Improve**: feed flagged examples back into prompts, retrieval data or fine-tuning, then re-evaluate against the same set to confirm the fix.

An average score that looks fine can hide a group that is consistently served worse, so look at the slices.

sections.heading: Audit trails and regulation
sections.body:
**Audit trails** record who asked what, which rails fired, which tools ran with which arguments, who approved them, and which model and config version answered. Logs should be tamper-evident, access-controlled and redacted, and kept as long as policy requires. Together with versioned guardrail configs, they let you reconstruct and justify any decision.

**Regulation** is risk-based. The EU AI Act is now **adopted law (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)**, not a proposal, even though some study material still calls it one. Its themes are risk tiers, transparency, human oversight, and documentation for higher-risk uses. Sector regulators such as the FDA (for AI in medical devices) add domain rules. Also respect **licensing**: check the licence terms of every model, dataset and library you ship.

keyPoints: Indirect injection arrives through retrieved documents and tool output. Treat both as untrusted data.
Least-privilege tools plus human approval for side-effecting actions limit the damage when an injection succeeds.
Mask PII on input and output, and redact logs and traces.
Measure bias per slice on a fixed eval set, filter toxicity with output rails, and re-evaluate after each fix.
Audit trails capture requests, rail decisions, tool calls, approvals and model/config versions.
The EU AI Act is adopted law (2024/1689): risk tiers, transparency, human oversight.

gotchas.trap: The EU AI Act is still a proposal.
gotchas.correct: It was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Obligations phase in over time.

gotchas.trap: Logging full prompts and responses unredacted is fine for an audit trail.
gotchas.correct: Audit logs can themselves leak PII. Redact them and restrict access.

gotchas.trap: A good overall toxicity score means the system is unbiased.
gotchas.correct: Aggregates hide per-group disparities. Evaluate by slice.

lessons.title: Human-in-the-Loop Approval and Escalation
lessons.summary: Where to put humans in an agent's control flow: approval gates before irreversible actions, confidence- and risk-based escalation, interrupt-and-resume on checkpointed state, and the protocol hooks (A2A Input Required, MCP Elicitation) that carry a request for human input.

sections.heading: Why oversight is a design concern, not an afterthought
sections.body:
The NCP-AAI study guide gives Domain 10 four subtopics: intuitive UIs with **user-in-the-loop** interaction, **structured feedback loops**, **transparency** (explainable reasoning and decision traceability), and **human oversight and intervention** for accountability and trust.

An agent that can call tools can change the world: send email, move money, delete records, open tickets. The more autonomy and side effects it has, the more you need explicit points where a human can see what is about to happen and stop it. Oversight is cheapest when it is built into the workflow graph from the start rather than bolted on after an incident.

sections.heading: Approval gates before irreversible actions
sections.body:
An **approval gate** pauses the agent *before* a side-effecting or irreversible step and shows a human exactly what will happen (the tool, its arguments, and the reason). The human approves, edits, or rejects.

Good practice:
- Gate by **risk**, not by every step. Read-only lookups usually run freely; refunds above a threshold, deletions, external messages and production changes are gated.
- Show the **concrete action**, such as `issue_refund(order=1832, amount=480.00)`, not a vague "May I proceed?".
- Let the reviewer **edit** the arguments, not just say yes or no.
- Log who approved what, and when, so the decision is auditable.

Gating everything causes approval fatigue: reviewers start clicking "approve" without reading, which is worse than a well-chosen gate.

sections.heading: Escalation: confidence, risk and failure
sections.body:
**Escalation** hands the task (or one decision) to a human when the agent should not continue alone. Common triggers:
- **Low confidence**: retrieval found nothing relevant, a classifier score is below threshold, or the agent's answers disagree across samples.
- **High stakes**: legal, medical, financial or safety-relevant requests, or requests that a policy says need a human.
- **Repeated failure**: tool errors after retries, or a circuit breaker is open. A human handoff is a legitimate fallback for graceful degradation.
- **User request**: the user asks for a person.

The handoff should carry context (conversation, plan so far, tool results) so the human does not start from zero. Track the **escalation rate** as a reliability metric: a sudden rise often signals drift or a broken tool.

sections.heading: Interrupt and resume on checkpointed state
sections.body:
In a stateful graph orchestrator (the LangGraph-style pattern covered in Domain 1), shared state is **checkpointed** per thread. A human-in-the-loop step **interrupts** the graph at a node, persists the state, and waits. When the human responds, hours later if needed, the graph **resumes from the checkpoint** with the human's input merged in, rather than re-running earlier steps or re-calling tools that already had side effects.

This is why durable checkpointing matters for oversight: without it, a pause for approval either blocks a worker indefinitely or loses the run.

sections.heading: Protocol-level hooks for asking a human
sections.body:
Agent protocols carry HITL natively:
- **A2A**: a task can enter the **Input Required** state (or **Auth Required**). These are *interrupted*, non-terminal states; the client supplies the missing input and the task continues. Completed, Failed, Canceled and Rejected are terminal.
- **MCP**: **Elicitation** is a client feature that lets a server request information from the user through the client. MCP's security principles also call for **user consent before tool invocation** and treat tool annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted.

Use these instead of inventing an ad-hoc "please reply with..." convention in free text.

keyPoints: Gate side-effecting and irreversible actions; let read-only steps run without approval.
Show the exact tool call and arguments to the approver, and allow edits.
Escalate on low confidence, high stakes, repeated failure, or user request, and pass full context.
Interrupt-and-resume relies on checkpointed graph state so approved runs continue without redoing side effects.
A2A Input Required and MCP Elicitation are protocol-level HITL mechanisms.
Escalation rate is a reliability metric worth alerting on.

gotchas.trap: Require human approval on every step to be safe.
gotchas.correct: Gate by risk. Blanket approval causes fatigue and rubber-stamping; gate irreversible or high-impact actions.

gotchas.trap: Ask the agent to confirm in its own reply that the action is safe.
gotchas.correct: Self-confirmation is not oversight. The pause must be enforced by the orchestrator before the tool executes.

gotchas.trap: A2A Input Required is a terminal failure state.
gotchas.correct: Input Required (and Auth Required) are interrupted states; the task resumes once input is supplied.

gotchas.trap: After approval, restart the workflow from the beginning.
gotchas.correct: Resume from the checkpoint so earlier tool calls are not repeated.

lessons.lab: Sketch a refund agent as a graph: lookup_order, decide_refund, issue_refund, notify_customer. Mark which nodes need an approval gate, define two escalation triggers with thresholds, and describe what state must be checkpointed so the run can resume after a reviewer approves the next morning.

lessons.title: Transparency, Explainability and Feedback Loops
lessons.summary: How to make agent behavior understandable and correctable: surfacing plans, sources and tool calls, decision traceability through traces and audit logs, user-facing explanations versus raw reasoning, and structured feedback that flows into the evaluation set (the data flywheel).

sections.heading: What users should be able to see
sections.body:
Transparency means a user or operator can understand **what the agent did and why**. Practical mechanisms:
- **Show the plan** for multi-step tasks before or while executing it.
- **Cite sources** for retrieved facts so claims can be checked.
- **Surface tool calls** ("Searched orders for #1832", "Created ticket INC-552") so side effects are never invisible.
- **State uncertainty** and limits plainly ("I could not find a policy covering this; routing to an agent").
- **Disclose that the user is talking to an AI.** Transparency and human oversight are core principles in AI regulation such as the EU AI Act, which is adopted law, not a proposal.

sections.heading: Explainable reasoning without dumping raw chain-of-thought
sections.body:
Chain-of-thought prompting can improve multi-step reasoning, and a ReAct loop (Thought, Action, Observation) gives a natural record of steps. But a raw reasoning transcript is not automatically a good explanation: it can be long, contain internal details or sensitive data, and does not guarantee the model's stated reasons are faithful.

Prefer a **concise, user-facing rationale** grounded in evidence: the sources used, the rule applied, and the action taken. Keep the full step-by-step trace for operators and auditors, with sensitive fields redacted.

sections.heading: Decision traceability
sections.body:
**Traceability** means any decision can be reconstructed after the fact. Record each run as a trace with spans for every LLM call, tool call, retrieval and guardrail check, plus inputs, outputs, model version, prompt version, and the human approvals or overrides that occurred.

NeMo Agent Toolkit (NAT) provides observability and profiling for workflows, and NeMo Guardrails can enforce input, dialog, retrieval, execution and output rails whose decisions also belong in the trace. With this in place you can answer "why did the agent refund this customer?" with evidence rather than guesswork.

*Current status:* NAT was deprecated in October 2026 (successors: NeMo Relay, Helix, Fabric), but the exam guide still teaches NAT.

sections.heading: Intuitive UIs and user-in-the-loop interaction
sections.body:
The interface is where oversight actually happens. NAT ships a built-in chat UI and an API server (`nat serve`) for interacting with workflows. Whatever UI you use, design for intervention:
- clear approve / edit / reject controls on proposed actions
- a visible **stop** or cancel control for long-running tasks
- streaming progress so users can catch a wrong turn early
- an obvious path to a human.

sections.heading: Structured feedback and the data flywheel
sections.body:
Free-text complaints are hard to act on. **Structured feedback** captures a rating (thumbs up/down or a scale) plus a **reason code** (wrong answer, missing source, unsafe, too slow) and stores it **with the trace** of the run it describes.

That linkage enables a **data flywheel**: production interactions and feedback are triaged, the failures become new **evaluation cases**, prompts, tools or models are improved, and the change is re-evaluated before release. NAT's evaluation tooling (`nat eval`) runs a workflow against a dataset, so routing curated failures into that dataset closes the loop. Human overrides at approval gates are equally valuable signals: every rejected action is a labeled example of what the agent should not do.

keyPoints: Show plan, sources and tool calls; never hide side effects from users.
Give concise evidence-based rationales to users; keep full traces for operators and auditors.
Trace every LLM, tool, retrieval and guardrail step with versions and human approvals.
UIs need approve/edit/reject, stop/cancel, streaming progress and a human handoff path.
Structured feedback (rating plus reason code) stored with the trace feeds the eval set: the data flywheel.
Teach NAT as exam content; it is deprecated in current NVIDIA tooling.

gotchas.trap: Showing the full raw chain-of-thought is the best explainability mechanism.
gotchas.correct: Raw reasoning can be noisy, sensitive and not faithful. Give a grounded rationale with sources; keep detailed traces for audit.

gotchas.trap: Collect feedback as free-text comments in a separate survey tool.
gotchas.correct: Store a structured rating and reason code linked to the run's trace so failures can become eval cases.

gotchas.trap: Feed all thumbs-down conversations straight into fine-tuning.
gotchas.correct: Triage and label first, add to the eval set, and re-evaluate changes before release.

lessons.lab: Design the feedback widget and trace schema for a support agent: list the reason codes, the trace fields a reviewer needs to reproduce a bad answer, and the weekly process that turns flagged runs into new evaluation cases.
