flashcards.front: Reactive agent architecture
flashcards.back: Maps stimulus straight to response with no planning or world model. Fast, cheap and predictable, but cannot pursue multi-step goals.

flashcards.front: Deliberative agent architecture
flashcards.back: Plans toward goals using a model of the world or task. Handles multi-step and novel problems at the cost of latency and complexity.

flashcards.front: Hybrid agent architecture
flashcards.back: A reactive layer handles time-critical inputs while a deliberative planner pursues longer-horizon goals on top.

flashcards.front: The ReAct loop
flashcards.back: Thought (reason about next step), Action (tool call), Observation (tool result appended to context), repeated until a final answer.

flashcards.front: Why ReAct reduces hallucination
flashcards.back: Each reasoning step is grounded in real observations from tools rather than the model's unverified internal knowledge.

flashcards.front: ReWOO vs ReAct
flashcards.back: ReWOO plans all tool calls up front then executes and solves, using fewer LLM calls; ReAct re-reasons after every observation and adapts better.

flashcards.front: Three safety controls for any agent loop
flashcards.back: A maximum-iteration cap, an explicit stop condition, and tool errors returned to the model as observations.

flashcards.front: Prompt chain
flashcards.back: A fixed sequence of LLM calls where each output feeds the next; developer-defined, predictable and easy to test.

flashcards.front: Logic tree / router
flashcards.back: A classifier or rule chooses which predefined branch (chain or agent) handles an input; should include a fallback branch.

flashcards.front: "Least autonomy" design principle
flashcards.back: Use a chain or router when the path is known in advance; reserve free agent loops for tasks whose steps cannot be planned ahead.

flashcards.front: Stateful graph orchestration: four parts
flashcards.back: Nodes (steps), edges including conditional ones (control flow), shared state, and checkpoints (persisted state per thread ID). Cycles allow bounded retry/reflection.

flashcards.front: What checkpointing enables
flashcards.back: Resuming multi-turn tasks, recovering from crashes at the last step, interrupting for human approval, and auditing how a result was reached.

flashcards.front: Short-term vs long-term agent memory
flashcards.back: Short-term: working context and task state, managed by trimming or summarising. Long-term: external store (episodic, semantic, procedural) retrieved across sessions.

flashcards.front: Supervisor (orchestrator-worker) pattern
flashcards.back: A central agent delegates subtasks to specialist workers and synthesises their outputs into one accountable result.

flashcards.front: When to use a hierarchical multi-agent design
flashcards.back: When a single supervisor would manage too many workers or too much context: group workers into teams, each with its own supervisor.

flashcards.front: Parallel fan-out / fan-in
flashcards.back: Independent subtasks run concurrently and an aggregator merges results, cutting end-to-end latency.

flashcards.front: A2A Agent Card
flashcards.back: JSON metadata at /.well-known/agent-card.json describing an agent's skills, capabilities (streaming, push notifications) and security schemes, used for discovery.

flashcards.front: A2A task states
flashcards.back: Submitted, Working; interrupted: Input Required, Auth Required; terminal: Completed, Failed, Canceled, Rejected.

flashcards.front: A2A vs MCP
flashcards.back: MCP connects an agent to tools, resources and prompts; A2A connects an agent to another opaque agent that plans its own work.

flashcards.front: A2A opacity principle
flashcards.back: Agents collaborate by exchanging tasks, messages and artifacts without access to each other's internal state, memory or tools.

flashcards.front: Knowledge graph vs vector store
flashcards.back: Vector stores find semantically similar text; knowledge graphs traverse typed relationships for multi-hop, relational questions. GraphRAG combines both.

flashcards.front: Human-agent UI essentials
flashcards.back: Stream progress, show plan, sources and tool calls, gate irreversible actions behind approval, ask for missing info, allow interrupt and escalation.

flashcards.front: Stateless agent workers
flashcards.back: Keep session and checkpoint state in a shared external store so any replica can serve any request, enabling horizontal scaling.

flashcards.front: NeMo Agent Toolkit built-in agent types
flashcards.back: ReAct, ReWOO, Reasoning, Router, Tool Calling, and Sequential and Parallel Executor agents, selected in YAML workflow config.

flashcards.front: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
flashcards.back: Closed (calls pass and failures are counted), Open (calls fail fast for a cool-down period) and Half-Open (limited trial calls decide whether to close or reopen).

flashcards.front: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
flashcards.back: Randomising the delay stops many clients from retrying at the same moment, which would cause a thundering herd against a service that is recovering.

flashcards.front: Which operations are safe to retry automatically?
flashcards.back: Idempotent or otherwise safe operations. Writes need an idempotency key or another duplicate guard first.

flashcards.front: Which errors should not be retried?
flashcards.back: Non-transient errors such as validation failures (400) or authentication errors, because retrying gives the same result.

flashcards.front: How should retry and circuit breaker patterns work together?
flashcards.back: Retry logic checks the breaker and stops retrying while the breaker is open, so it doesn't hammer a dependency that is down.

flashcards.front: Name three graceful-degradation fallbacks for an agent.
flashcards.back: Serve a cached answer, fall back to a simpler or smaller model, or hand off to a human with context. Skipping optional steps is another.

flashcards.front: What should an agent loop do when a tool raises an exception?
flashcards.back: Catch it and return a structured error as the observation so the model can re-plan or pick another tool. Bound the loop with a maximum number of iterations.

flashcards.front: What makes a prompt chain 'dynamic'?
flashcards.back: The next step or prompt is chosen at runtime from earlier outputs, for example an intent classifier routing to a specialised prompt.

flashcards.front: Main benefit of splitting a large prompt into a chain?
flashcards.back: Each step is focused and testable, outputs can be validated between steps, a different model can be used per step, and failures point to one step.

flashcards.front: What is p-tuning?
flashcards.back: A parameter-efficient method: a small model learns task-specific virtual-token (soft prompt) embeddings that are prepended to the prompt, while the base LLM's weights stay frozen.

flashcards.front: Which NIM model categories support multimodal agents?
flashcards.back: Vision Language Models (VLMs), Speech (Riva) for speech recognition and text-to-speech, and NV-CLIP for shared image-text embeddings.

flashcards.front: What is NV-CLIP used for in an agent?
flashcards.back: Embedding images and text in a shared space, so a text query can retrieve relevant images (cross-modal search).

flashcards.front: In tool calling, what does the model actually produce?
flashcards.back: A structured call with a tool name and JSON arguments that should match the tool's JSON Schema. The application validates the arguments and runs the tool.

flashcards.front: Two ways to reduce wrong tool calls?
flashcards.back: Write clear tool descriptions (when to use it and when not to) and constrain parameters with typed schemas, enums and formats. Then validate on the server.

flashcards.front: How are custom tools registered in the NeMo Agent Toolkit?
flashcards.back: As Functions or Function Groups, composed into workflows through YAML workflow configuration.

flashcards.front: Which protocol integrations does NAT provide?
flashcards.back: An MCP client and server (including FastMCP) and an A2A client and server, plus plugins for frameworks such as LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex and CrewAI.

flashcards.front: What are the three MCP server features?
flashcards.back: Tools (functions the model runs), Resources (context and data) and Prompts (templated messages).

flashcards.front: ReAct vs ReWOO, in one line each?
flashcards.back: ReAct alternates Thought, Action and Observation and re-decides after every tool result. ReWOO plans all tool calls first and then executes them, using fewer LLM calls.

flashcards.front: Two kinds of streaming that improve a long agent run's UX?
flashcards.back: Token streaming (often over SSE) and intermediate step events that show which tool or step is running.

flashcards.front: How should user feedback be captured to improve an agent?
flashcards.back: As structured signals, such as thumbs up or down with reason codes, stored with the trace of that run so failures can be found and added to eval sets.

flashcards.front: Which NAT evaluator scores an agent's tool-use path?
flashcards.back: The trajectory evaluator, an LLM judge of the agent's sequence of tool calls, run through nat eval.

flashcards.front: What does `nat eval --config_file=workflow.yml` do?
flashcards.back: It runs the workflow over the configured dataset and scores the results with every evaluator listed under `eval.evaluators`, writing outputs to `eval.general.output_dir`.

flashcards.front: Default value of `eval.general.max_concurrency` in NAT evaluation?
Recommended ragas metrics in NAT evaluation
flashcards.back: AnswerAccuracy, ContextRelevance and ResponseGroundedness, each scored 0 to 1. FactualCorrectness is also available.

flashcards.front: What does the `trajectory` evaluator score?
flashcards.back: An LLM judge scores the agent's tool-use trajectory, meaning the sequence of steps and tool calls, not just the final answer.

flashcards.front: What does `tunable_rag_evaluator` score?
flashcards.back: Coverage, Correctness and Relevance, with weights you can change or a custom judge prompt.

flashcards.front: `nat eval --skip_workflow --dataset=<file>`
flashcards.back: Scores outputs that already exist in the dataset, offline, without running the agent again.

flashcards.front: `nat eval --skip_completed_entries`
flashcards.back: Resumes an interrupted evaluation run by skipping items that already have results.

flashcards.front: `nat eval --endpoint http://localhost:8000`
flashcards.back: Evaluates a remote workflow started with `nat serve` instead of running it locally.

flashcards.front: Why use `nat eval --reps=N`?
flashcards.back: To repeat the run N times and measure run-to-run variance before comparing agents.

flashcards.front: `config_original.yml` vs `config_effective.yml`
flashcards.back: Original is the config as written. Effective is the config after CLI overrides were applied, so use it to reproduce or audit a run.

flashcards.front: How do you list the evaluators available in a NAT environment?
flashcards.back: `nat info components -t evaluator`.

flashcards.front: What does profiler `prompt_caching_prefixes` find?
flashcards.back: Shared prompt prefixes across requests that are candidates for KV-cache reuse.

flashcards.front: What is in `inference_optimization.json`?
flashcards.back: Latency, throughput and runtime estimates with 90%, 95% and 99% confidence intervals.

flashcards.front: What does `@track_function` do in NAT?
flashcards.back: It instruments an arbitrary Python function so the profiler records its calls and timing.

flashcards.front: What does `nat sizing calc` estimate?
flashcards.back: The GPU cluster size needed to serve a target number of users within a target response time. It is the Sizing Calculator.

flashcards.front: What makes user feedback structured?
flashcards.back: A fixed signal (thumbs or rating) plus reason codes, stored with the trace or request ID so reviewed cases can become new eval items.

flashcards.front: How do clients call an NVIDIA NIM for LLMs?
flashcards.back: Through an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API, for example /v1/chat/completions, served by the NIM container. Existing OpenAI-style clients usually only need a new base URL and model name.

flashcards.front: What is NIM_CACHE_PATH and why mount it?
flashcards.back: The model cache location inside the NIM container (default /opt/nim/.cache). Mount persistent storage there, or the model downloads again on every start, which makes cold starts and scale-out slow.

flashcards.front: How do you see and pin a NIM model profile?
flashcards.back: List profiles with list-model-profiles, and set NIM_MODEL_PROFILE to override the automatic engine and hardware choice.

flashcards.front: What manages NIM deployments on Kubernetes?
flashcards.back: The NVIDIA NIM Operator, which manages NIM microservices on Kubernetes declaratively.

flashcards.front: What credential does a NIM container need to pull models?
flashcards.back: An NGC API key. NIM is distributed as part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise.

flashcards.front: Which metrics should drive autoscaling of LLM serving pods?
flashcards.back: GPU utilization and request-queue depth, exported with the DCGM exporter into kube-prometheus. CPU alone is a weak signal for GPU-bound inference.

flashcards.front: What is NVIDIA Dynamo?
flashcards.back: An open-source distributed inference framework that runs above vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. It provides disaggregated serving, KV-aware routing, NIXL KV transfer and an SLO-driven Planner.

flashcards.front: What is disaggregated prefill/decode serving?
flashcards.back: Running the prompt-processing (prefill) phase and the token-generation (decode) phase on separate workers, so heavy prefills do not stall decoding. Dynamo supports it.

flashcards.front: What does NIXL do in Dynamo?
flashcards.back: It transfers KV cache between workers, for example from prefill workers to decode workers.

flashcards.front: What is KV-aware routing?
flashcards.back: Routing a request to a worker that already holds the relevant KV cache, such as a shared system prompt, so the prefix does not have to be recomputed.

flashcards.front: Triton dynamic batcher: what does max_queue_delay_microseconds do?
flashcards.back: It lets the server hold requests briefly to build a larger batch. When the delay expires, the batch is sent as it is. The docs advise usually leaving preferred_batch_size unset.

flashcards.front: When do you use the Triton sequence batcher?
flashcards.back: For stateful models. It routes every request in a sequence to the same model instance.

flashcards.front: What is Triton Inference Server called now?
flashcards.back: NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton, part of the Dynamo platform. Older material, including the study guide, says Triton Inference Server.

flashcards.front: What does the NAT profiler file inference_optimization.json contain?
flashcards.back: Latency, throughput and runtime figures with 90/95/99% confidence intervals for the profiled workflow.

flashcards.front: Which NAT profiler options help find bottlenecks under concurrency?
flashcards.back: bottleneck_analysis (nested-stack or simple-stack) and concurrency_spike_analysis (with spike_threshold), plus the Gantt chart output.

flashcards.front: What does prompt_caching_prefixes in the NAT profiler find?
flashcards.back: Shared prompt prefixes across calls that are good candidates for prompt/KV-cache reuse. It is a cost and latency lever.

flashcards.front: What does nat sizing calc do?
flashcards.back: It runs the NAT Sizing Calculator, which estimates the GPU cluster size a workflow needs for a target number of users and workflow runtime.

flashcards.front: What is an evaluation gate in agent CI/CD?
flashcards.back: A pipeline step that runs automated evaluation (such as nat eval on a golden dataset) and blocks promotion when quality regresses against the baseline.

flashcards.front: What should be versioned together in an agent release?
flashcards.back: Prompt templates, tool definitions and schemas, model identifiers and profiles, and workflow config. Together they let you reproduce and roll back behavior.

flashcards.front: Canary vs blue-green deployment?
flashcards.back: Canary sends a small traffic slice to the new version and compares metrics before widening. Blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments. Both allow fast rollback.

flashcards.front: What are the five planning families in the LLM-agent planning survey (arXiv:2402.02716)?
flashcards.back: Task decomposition, multi-plan selection, external-module-aided planning, reflection and refinement, and memory-augmented planning.

flashcards.front: Decompose-first vs interleaved decomposition?
flashcards.back: Decompose-first writes all sub-goals up front then executes; interleaved decides the next sub-goal after each result. Interleaved adapts better, decompose-first is cheaper and easier to inspect.

flashcards.front: What does chain-of-thought prompting do, and what can it not do?
flashcards.back: It elicits intermediate reasoning steps, improving multi-step reasoning. It cannot access information outside the context; that needs tools or retrieval.

flashcards.front: Self-consistency
flashcards.back: Sample several chain-of-thought reasoning paths and take the majority final answer. A form of multi-plan selection.

flashcards.front: ReAct vs ReWOO in one line each
flashcards.back: ReAct: Thought, Action, Observation per step; adaptive but more LLM calls. ReWOO: plan all tool calls first, execute, then solve; fewer calls but less adaptive mid-run.

flashcards.front: Plan-and-execute with re-planning
flashcards.back: An explicit step list is executed step by step; when a step fails or new information appears, the planner revises the remaining plan.

flashcards.front: What makes reflection effective?
flashcards.back: An external signal (test failure, validation error, tool error, grader score) plus a cap on rounds. Reflexion stores verbal reflections in episodic memory for later attempts.

flashcards.front: Short-term memory management strategies
flashcards.back: Sliding window or trimming, running summarization, pinned structured state for critical facts, and compacting large tool outputs to references.

flashcards.front: Episodic vs semantic vs procedural memory
flashcards.back: Episodic: past interactions and events. Semantic: facts and knowledge (vector or graph store). Procedural: learned how-to, such as workflows and successful plans.

flashcards.front: Memory vs checkpointed orchestration state
flashcards.back: Memory holds knowledge to recall; checkpointed state holds task progress (completed steps, pending inputs) keyed by thread ID so the run can resume.

flashcards.front: Why key checkpoints by thread or session ID?
flashcards.back: Each conversation or job resumes its own state, concurrent users stay isolated, and human-in-the-loop pauses can resume later.

flashcards.front: NeMo Agent Toolkit Automatic Memory Wrapper
flashcards.back: An agent type that wraps another agent to add automatic memory retrieval and storage, with pluggable memory backends (Redis via the nemo-agent-toolkit-redis package).

flashcards.front: In-context learning
flashcards.back: A large model picks up a task pattern from examples in the prompt without weight updates, which is why retrieved past examples or reflections can steer an agent.

flashcards.front: What is NVIDIA NeMo Retriever?
flashcards.back: A family of NIM microservices for RAG pipelines: multimodal extraction (nv-ingest), text embedding, and text reranking.

flashcards.front: What does NeMo Retriever extraction (nv-ingest) do?
flashcards.back: Pulls text, tables, charts and images out of documents, runs via nv-ingest-cli or a Python API, and ingests results into Milvus.

flashcards.front: What is nemoretriever-parse used for?
flashcards.back: Parsing scanned pages and complex document layouts during NeMo Retriever extraction.

flashcards.front: Embedding model vs reranking model: what is the difference?
flashcards.back: An embedder encodes queries and passages separately into vectors for fast similarity search. A reranker (cross-encoder) scores each query-passage pair together to reorder a small candidate set more precisely.

flashcards.front: Why can a reranker not fix poor recall?
flashcards.back: It only reorders the candidates the first-stage retriever returned; if the right passage is not in that set, reranking cannot surface it.

flashcards.front: What problem does hybrid search solve?
flashcards.back: Dense retrieval misses exact tokens (part numbers, error codes, names); combining keyword search such as BM25 with dense vectors catches both exact terms and paraphrases.

flashcards.front: HNSW vs IVF
flashcards.back: Both are approximate nearest neighbor indexes. HNSW navigates a layered proximity graph (fast, high recall, more memory); IVF clusters vectors and searches only the nearest clusters. Both trade recall for latency via tunable parameters.

flashcards.front: What happens if you change the embedding model for queries but not documents?
flashcards.back: Retrieval breaks: vectors from different models are in different spaces. Re-embed the corpus with the new model before switching.

flashcards.front: RAG or fine-tuning?
flashcards.back: RAG for fresh or proprietary facts and citations; fine-tuning for style, format or domain behavior. They can be combined.

flashcards.front: When should an agent use a knowledge graph instead of vector search?
flashcards.back: For relational and multi-hop questions where the answer depends on traversing relationships between entities.

flashcards.front: What does GraphRAG add over plain vector RAG?
flashcards.back: An LLM-extracted entity graph with community summaries, enabling both local (entity-neighborhood) and global (whole-corpus theme) questions.

flashcards.front: How should an agent answer from a data warehouse?
flashcards.back: Through a guarded query tool (for example read-only text-to-SQL with schema context), not by embedding table rows.

flashcards.front: Three ways to keep agent knowledge fresh
flashcards.back: Incremental upserts and deletes keyed by document ID and timestamp; change data capture for fast-changing sources; live API tools for real-time data.

flashcards.front: Name four data quality checks before indexing
flashcards.back: Near-duplicate removal, boilerplate stripping, encoding/empty-chunk checks, metadata completeness (source, date, access tags), plus PII handling per policy.

flashcards.front: Which study guide Domain 6 subtopics go beyond retrieval?
flashcards.back: 6.3 ETL pipelines for enterprise or client data, and 6.4 data quality checks, augmentation and preprocessing.

flashcards.front: NVIDIA NIM: what is it, and what API does it expose?
flashcards.back: A prebuilt, optimized inference microservice container for a model. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, e.g. /v1/chat/completions.

flashcards.front: TensorRT-LLM: what does it provide?
flashcards.back: An engine and library that optimizes LLM inference: optimized kernels, quantization (FP8/FP4/INT4), in-flight batching and paged KV cache.

flashcards.front: What is Triton Inference Server called now, and what is it for?
flashcards.back: NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton. A general model server with multi-framework backends, dynamic batching and ensembles.

flashcards.front: When do you reach for NVIDIA Dynamo?
flashcards.back: When you serve an LLM across many GPUs or nodes. It offers disaggregated prefill/decode, KV-aware routing and KV-cache transfer via NIXL, and runs above vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM.

flashcards.front: Triton dynamic batcher vs sequence batcher?
flashcards.back: The dynamic batcher combines stateless requests on the server (tuned with max_queue_delay_microseconds). The sequence batcher sends every request in a stateful sequence to the same model instance.

flashcards.front: Why mount NIM_CACHE_PATH?
flashcards.back: It persists the downloaded model (default /opt/nim/.cache). Without it, the NIM downloads the model again on every container start.

flashcards.front: How do you pin a NIM to a specific engine/hardware configuration?
flashcards.back: Run list-model-profiles to see the options, then set NIM_MODEL_PROFILE. Otherwise NIM picks a profile automatically.

flashcards.front: NeMo Guardrails: the five rail types?
flashcards.back: Input, retrieval, dialog, execution and output.

flashcards.front: NeMo Guardrails: what language defines flows, and what defines models and rails?
flashcards.back: Colang defines flows. config.yml sets models, prompts, rails and tracing. Custom actions are Python functions.

flashcards.front: NeMo Agent Toolkit: package, CLI and earlier names?
flashcards.back: Package nvidia-nat, CLI nat. Earlier names were AgentIQ and Agent Intelligence Toolkit (aiqtoolkit, CLI aiq).

flashcards.front: What does NAT add to an existing LangGraph or CrewAI agent?
flashcards.back: Framework-agnostic YAML wiring, evaluation (nat eval), profiling (token and latency bottlenecks), MCP/A2A clients and servers, and nat serve. You keep your existing framework.

flashcards.front: What is an NVIDIA Blueprint?
flashcards.back: A reference workflow (code, deployment configs and docs) that combines NIM and NeMo components for one use case, such as AI-Q research or a RAG pipeline. You customize it.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a trace and a span in agent observability?
flashcards.back: A trace is one end-to-end agent run; spans are its nested steps (each LLM call, tool call, retrieval or guardrail check), each with its own latency, tokens and errors.

flashcards.front: Which telemetry standard do NeMo Agent Toolkit's Observe Workflows exporters build on?
flashcards.back: OpenTelemetry. NAT also has native LangSmith integration.

flashcards.front: Which MCP _meta keys are reserved for distributed tracing?
flashcards.back: traceparent, tracestate and baggage (W3C trace context), so a client can pass trace context to an MCP server.

flashcards.front: Name five reliability metrics for an agent dashboard.
flashcards.back: Task success rate, tool-error rate, p95/p99 latency, groundedness (or answer accuracy), and escalation rate. Tokens/cost per request is a useful sixth.

flashcards.front: A RAG agent hallucinates. What should you check first?
flashcards.back: Retrieval: whether the relevant context was retrieved (context relevance). Only then check whether the answer stayed grounded in it.

flashcards.front: Which NAT ragas metrics separate retrieval problems from generation problems?
flashcards.back: ContextRelevance (retrieval quality) vs ResponseGroundedness (did the answer stick to the context), with AnswerAccuracy for the end result; each scores 0 to 1.

flashcards.front: How do you benchmark a new agent version against the previous one?
flashcards.back: Run the same evaluation (same golden dataset, same judge) on both versions, with repeated runs to measure variance, for example nat eval --reps=N.

flashcards.front: What does the NAT profiler collect?
flashcards.back: Per-invocation tokens, latency, and LLM and tool calls; @track_function instruments arbitrary functions. Outputs include profiler traces, a Gantt chart and bottleneck analysis.

flashcards.front: Transient vs persistent tool failure: how should each be handled?
flashcards.back: Transient (timeout, rate limit, 5xx): bounded retries with backoff plus a circuit breaker. Persistent (expired auth, changed schema): don't retry; alert and fail gracefully.

flashcards.front: What are the five NeMo Guardrails rail types?
flashcards.back: Input, dialog, retrieval, execution and output.

flashcards.front: Which rail type is aimed at indirect prompt injection from RAG documents?
flashcards.back: Retrieval rails. They filter or mask retrieved chunks before the model sees them.

flashcards.front: What does an execution rail check?
flashcards.back: Tool or action calls: their inputs and outputs, before and after they run.

flashcards.front: What language defines NeMo Guardrails flows, and which file declares models and rails?
flashcards.back: Colang defines flows. config.yml declares models, prompts, rails and tracing. Self-check prompts live in prompts.yml.

flashcards.front: Name the NemoGuard NIM roles used with NeMo Guardrails.
flashcards.back: Jailbreak detection, content safety and topic control. PII is handled by integrations such as Presidio and GLiNER-PII.

flashcards.front: What is indirect prompt injection?
flashcards.back: Malicious instructions hidden in content the agent reads, such as web pages, emails, retrieved chunks or tool output, rather than typed by the user.

flashcards.front: Two controls that limit damage if a prompt injection succeeds?
flashcards.back: Least-privilege tools and human approval before side-effecting or irreversible actions.

flashcards.front: What should an agent audit trail record?
flashcards.back: Requests, rail decisions, tool calls with arguments, approvals, and the model and config versions. It should be redacted and access-controlled.

flashcards.front: Is the EU AI Act still a proposal?
flashcards.back: No. It is adopted law, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, with risk-based obligations phasing in over time.

flashcards.front: What is an approval gate in an agent workflow?
flashcards.back: A pause enforced by the orchestrator before a side-effecting or irreversible tool call, where a human sees the exact action and arguments and approves, edits or rejects it.

flashcards.front: Name four common escalation triggers for an agent.
flashcards.back: Low confidence (weak retrieval, low classifier score), high-stakes requests, repeated tool failure after retries, and the user asking for a human.

flashcards.front: What are A2A's interrupted (non-terminal) task states used for HITL?
flashcards.back: Input Required and Auth Required. The client supplies the missing input or credentials and the task continues.

flashcards.front: What is MCP Elicitation?
flashcards.back: A client feature that lets an MCP server request information from the user through the client: a protocol-level human-in-the-loop hook.

flashcards.front: Why does interrupt-and-resume depend on checkpointing?
flashcards.back: The graph state is persisted at the interrupt so the run can resume after human input without re-running earlier steps or repeating side effects.

flashcards.front: What makes user feedback 'structured'?
flashcards.back: A rating plus a reason code, stored with the trace of the run it describes, so it can be triaged and turned into evaluation cases.

flashcards.front: What is the data flywheel?
flashcards.back: A loop where production interactions and feedback are curated into eval and training data, the agent is improved, re-evaluated, and redeployed.

flashcards.front: What does decision traceability require?
flashcards.back: A trace of every LLM call, tool call, retrieval and guardrail decision, with inputs/outputs, model and prompt versions, and human approvals or overrides.

flashcards.front: Why prefer a grounded rationale over raw chain-of-thought for users?
flashcards.back: Raw reasoning can be long, expose internal or sensitive details, and may not faithfully reflect why the model acted; a short evidence-based explanation is clearer and checkable.

questions.scenario: A logistics company is building an agent for autonomous warehouse robots. The robot must stop within milliseconds when a proximity sensor fires, and it must also plan multi-step pick routes that change as orders arrive.
questions.stem: Which architecture best fits these requirements?
options: A purely reactive architecture driven by sensor rules
A purely deliberative architecture that re-plans before every action
A hybrid architecture with a reactive safety layer beneath a deliberative route planner
A single prompt chain that runs once per order
questions.explanation: The scenario combines a hard real-time reflex with multi-step goal pursuit. A hybrid architecture lets a reactive layer handle the safety stop immediately while a deliberative layer plans routes. Either pure style fails one of the two requirements.
rationales: Reactive rules handle the stop but cannot plan multi-step routes that adapt to new orders.
Re-planning before every action adds latency the safety stop cannot afford.
Correct: reactive reflexes for safety plus deliberative planning for routes.
A one-shot chain neither reacts in real time nor re-plans as orders change.

questions.scenario: An HR team wants an internal assistant that answers about 40 well-defined policy questions (leave balance rules, holiday calendar, expense limits). Answers come from a fixed policy document and never require calling multiple systems.
questions.stem: An engineer proposes a deliberative planning agent with a ReAct loop and several tools. What is the best response?
options: Approve it, because deliberative agents give the most accurate answers in every case
Use a peer-to-peer multi-agent network so each policy area has its own agent
Remove retrieval entirely and rely on the model's general knowledge of HR policy
Use a simpler reactive design, such as intent routing to grounded single-step answers, because there are no multi-step goals
questions.explanation: With fixed intents and no multi-step goals, planning adds latency, cost and failure modes without benefit. A reactive design grounded in the policy document is cheaper, faster and more predictable. Choosing the least autonomy that solves the task is a core design principle.
rationales: Deliberation is not free; for single-step lookups it adds cost and risk without improving accuracy.
A multi-agent network multiplies coordination overhead for a trivial routing problem.
Company policy is proprietary; dropping grounding invites hallucinated answers.
Correct: a reactive, grounded design matches a fixed-intent, single-step workload.

questions.stem: In a ReAct agent, what happens immediately after the model emits an Action?
options: The planner discards the reasoning trace to save tokens
A human must approve every Action before the loop continues
The model writes its final answer without further input
The runtime executes the tool and appends the result to the context as an Observation
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves Thought, Action and Observation. After the model chooses an action, the runtime runs the tool and feeds the result back as an observation that the next thought must account for. That grounding is what distinguishes ReAct from reasoning alone.
rationales: The trace is kept; it conditions later steps and supports debugging.
Human approval is an optional design choice for risky actions, not part of the ReAct loop itself.
The loop continues after the observation; the final answer comes only when the model decides it has enough.
Correct: tool execution produces an Observation that is added to context.

questions.scenario: A reporting agent always needs the same four lookups (sales API, inventory API, budget sheet, forecast service) and the arguments for each are known from the user's request. The current ReAct implementation calls the LLM after every lookup and is too slow and expensive.
questions.stem: Which change most directly reduces LLM calls while keeping the same tools?
options: Replace the tools with a larger model that memorises the data
Switch to a ReWOO-style agent that plans all tool calls up front, executes them, then composes the answer
Increase the ReAct maximum iteration limit so the agent can finish in one run
Add a reflection step after each observation to improve accuracy
questions.explanation: When the tool plan does not depend on intermediate results, ReWOO separates planning from execution and avoids an LLM call per observation. ReAct's per-step reasoning is valuable only when results change the next step. NAT provides both agent types.
rationales: Live business data cannot be memorised and would go stale; grounding requires the tools.
Correct: planning once and executing all calls removes the per-observation LLM calls.
Raising the cap does not reduce calls per run; it only permits more.
Reflection adds LLM calls, making cost and latency worse.

questions.scenario: In production traces, a ReAct agent sometimes calls the same search tool with near-identical arguments 30+ times until the request times out, then returns nothing.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Switch the model temperature to the maximum to encourage variety
Raise the request timeout so the agent has time to finish
Add a maximum-iteration cap with a defined fallback, and detect repeated identical actions
Remove the search tool so the agent must answer directly
questions.explanation: Agent loops need explicit termination: an iteration cap, a stop condition and a fallback such as a partial answer or human handoff. Detecting repeated actions catches loops early. Longer timeouts only make the failure slower and costlier.
rationales: High temperature adds randomness and unreliability rather than fixing termination.
A longer timeout lets the loop burn more tokens before failing the same way.
Correct: bound the loop and handle the stuck case explicitly.
Removing the tool breaks the grounding the task needs.

questions.scenario: An insurer processes claim emails in exactly the same steps every time: extract fields, check them against policy rules, and produce a structured JSON summary. Errors in extraction currently surface only in the final JSON.
questions.stem: Which design is most appropriate?
options: A fully autonomous agent that decides which steps to run for each email
One large prompt that extracts, checks and formats in a single call
A peer-to-peer network of agents that negotiate the output
A prompt chain with one focused prompt per step and schema validation between steps
questions.explanation: The path is known in advance, so a prompt chain is more predictable and testable than an agent. Validation gates between steps catch bad intermediate output early instead of letting it poison later steps. Single mega-prompts are harder to debug.
rationales: Autonomy is unnecessary for a fixed path and makes behaviour less predictable.
A single call hides which step failed and is harder to test.
Negotiating agents add cost and nondeterminism to a deterministic job.
Correct: a fixed chain with validation gates matches a known workflow.

questions.scenario: A telecom support assistant handles billing disputes, technical outages and plan upgrades. Each category has its own validated workflow. About 5% of messages fit none of them.
questions.stem: Which orchestration approach is the best fit?
options: One general agent with every tool from all three workflows
Run all three workflows on every message and keep the longest answer
Ask the user to pick a workflow from a dropdown before typing anything
A router that classifies each message into the matching workflow, with a fallback branch to a human agent
questions.explanation: A logic tree or router keeps developer-validated paths while choosing one per input, and a fallback branch handles unclassifiable messages safely. NAT includes a Router agent for this pattern. One agent with every tool tends to choose tools less reliably as the list grows.
rationales: A single agent with a large mixed toolset loses the validated workflows and picks tools less reliably.
Running every branch wastes cost and has no sound way to pick the right answer.
Forcing manual selection hurts usability and still needs handling for misfits.
Correct: route to validated branches with an explicit fallback.

questions.scenario: A mortgage pre-approval agent collects documents over several days. Users leave and return, and the backend pods are restarted during deployments. Today the agent loses progress and asks users to start over.
questions.stem: Which design change best fixes this?
options: Increase the model context window so the whole history fits
Persist the orchestration graph state in checkpoints keyed by a thread ID and resume from the last checkpoint
Store the conversation in each pod's local memory and use sticky sessions
Ask users to paste their earlier answers when they return
questions.explanation: Stateful orchestration checkpoints shared state after each step, keyed by thread or session, so a multi-turn task can resume after pauses and restarts. A larger context window does not survive a pod restart. Local memory with sticky sessions is lost when the pod is replaced.
rationales: Context size does not persist anything across restarts or days.
Correct: durable checkpoints per thread let the task resume where it stopped.
Pod-local state disappears on restart, which is the failure being described.
Pushing state management onto users is a poor experience and error-prone.

questions.stem: A team is moving from a linear chain to graph-based stateful orchestration with conditional edges and checkpointed state. Which two benefits can they expect? (Select two.)
options: Deterministic LLM outputs regardless of temperature
No further need for an evaluation dataset
Bounded cycles that let a validator send work back for retry or reflection
The ability to pause for human approval and resume from the same state
questions.explanation: Graphs allow cycles, so a failed check can route back to an earlier node a bounded number of times. Checkpointed state lets the graph interrupt for a human and resume later. Orchestration controls flow; it does not make models deterministic or replace evaluation.
rationales: Model sampling is unaffected by how steps are orchestrated.
You still need evaluation to know whether the flow produces good results.
Correct: conditional edges and cycles enable retry and reflection loops.
Correct: checkpoints make interrupt-and-resume possible.

questions.scenario: A bank is designing fraud review. Separate specialist agents analyse transaction patterns, identity documents and device signals. Regulators require a single, explainable final decision with a record of which evidence drove it.
questions.stem: Which multi-agent topology best meets the requirement?
options: A peer network where agents vote and the majority label is final
Three independent agents that each message the customer directly
A sequential pipeline where each agent overwrites the previous agent's verdict
A supervisor (orchestrator-worker) pattern where a central agent delegates to specialists and synthesises one decision with cited evidence
questions.explanation: A supervisor delegates to specialists and combines their outputs into one accountable decision, which makes the evidence trail easy to record. Peer voting and parallel customer contact lack a single point of accountability. Overwriting verdicts discards evidence.
rationales: Majority voting hides how evidence was weighed and gives no single accountable reasoner.
Uncoordinated customer contact is confusing and unauditable.
Overwriting loses the earlier evidence regulators want recorded.
Correct: central synthesis gives one explainable decision and an audit trail.

questions.scenario: A travel agent must check flights, hotels and visa rules for a trip. The three lookups do not depend on each other, and users complain the agent takes too long because it runs them one after another.
questions.stem: Which change most improves latency?
options: Add a reflection step after each lookup
Merge the three tools into one tool with a very long description
Use a larger model for every step
Fan the three lookups out in parallel and aggregate the results
questions.explanation: Independent subtasks can run concurrently with a fan-out/fan-in pattern, so total latency approaches the slowest lookup instead of the sum. NAT offers a Parallel Executor for this. The other options add work or do not address sequential execution.
rationales: Reflection adds steps and latency.
A merged tool does not run lookups concurrently and makes tool selection harder.
Larger models are typically slower, not faster.
Correct: parallel execution removes the sequential wait.

questions.scenario: Your company's procurement agent needs to work with a supplier's autonomous quoting agent. The supplier's agent plans its own work, can take hours to finalise a quote, and runs on a different framework. The supplier will not expose its internal tools or memory.
questions.stem: Which integration approach fits best?
options: Wrap the supplier agent as an MCP tool and poll it synchronously in your agent loop
Communicate over the A2A protocol: discover it via its Agent Card and exchange tasks with streaming or push updates
Ask the supplier for read access to its agent's memory database
Scrape the supplier's web portal with a browser tool
questions.explanation: A2A is designed for opaque agent peers: they collaborate through tasks, messages and artifacts without sharing internal state, and long-running tasks report progress by streaming or push notification. MCP is for exposing tools and data to an agent. The NeMo Agent Toolkit includes A2A client and server support.
rationales: MCP suits tools and data; a long-running autonomous peer fits A2A's task lifecycle better than a synchronous tool call.
Correct: A2A provides discovery, task lifecycle and async updates between opaque agents.
The supplier will not share internals, and A2A does not require it.
Scraping is brittle and bypasses a proper agent interface.

sources.title: Agents and workflows — NeMo Agent Toolkit docs

questions.stem: You are publishing an internal research agent so other teams' agents can collaborate with it over an agent-to-agent protocol such as A2A. Which two design choices are appropriate? (Select two.)
options: Give calling agents direct access to the research agent's vector memory
Require every calling team to adopt the same agent framework you use
Publish discovery metadata that describes the agent's skills, capabilities and authentication requirements
Model long-running requests as tasks with explicit states and progress updates
questions.explanation: Agent-to-agent protocols rely on published capability metadata for discovery and on a task lifecycle with status updates for long work. Collaboration is opaque, so callers should not touch internal memory. Framework independence is a main reason to use a protocol.
rationales: Exposing internals breaks encapsulation and the opacity the protocol is designed around.
Protocols exist so agents built with different frameworks can interoperate.
Correct: discoverable capability and auth metadata lets other agents find and call it safely.
Correct: tasks with states and updates handle long-running work.

questions.scenario: A manufacturer asks its agent: "Which of our products would be affected if any supplier located in Region R stopped shipping?" Answering requires linking suppliers to components and components to products. A vector-only RAG system returns loosely related documents and misses most products.
questions.stem: What is the most effective architectural improvement?
options: Add a knowledge graph of suppliers, components and products that the agent can traverse, optionally combined with vector search
Fine-tune the model on supplier contracts
Shorten the chunk size in the vector index
Increase the vector top-k to retrieve more chunks
questions.explanation: This is a multi-hop relational question: supplier to component to product. Knowledge graphs store typed relationships so the agent can follow them explicitly, and GraphRAG combines graph traversal with vector entry points. Tuning similarity search does not reconstruct relationships that no single chunk contains.
rationales: Correct: graph traversal answers relational, multi-hop queries.
Fine-tuning does not keep supply relationships current or queryable.
Chunk size affects granularity, not the ability to chain relationships.
More chunks add noise; similarity search still does not follow relationships.

questions.scenario: A customer-service agent can issue refunds. Users say they do not trust it because it sometimes "just does things" and they cannot see why.
questions.stem: Which UI change best addresses this?
options: Add a disclaimer that the agent may make mistakes
Remove the refund tool entirely
Hide intermediate steps and show only the final message to keep the interface clean
Show the plan and tool calls as they stream, and require explicit user confirmation before issuing a refund
questions.explanation: Transparency (plan, sources, tool calls) and approval gates before irreversible actions are core human-agent interaction patterns. They let users verify what the agent intends and stay in control. A disclaimer alone changes nothing about control or visibility.
rationales: A disclaimer neither explains decisions nor prevents unwanted actions.
Removing the capability abandons the use case instead of making it safe.
Hiding activity is the cause of the distrust.
Correct: visible steps plus confirmation for side-effecting actions build trust and prevent mistakes.

questions.stem: Which two practices improve the interface of a multi-step agent that can take 30-60 seconds per request? (Select two.)
options: Require users to write their requests as JSON so they match the tool schema
Stream tokens and surface intermediate step updates while the agent works
Ask the user for missing required details instead of guessing them
Return nothing until the full answer is ready so users are not distracted
questions.explanation: Streaming progress keeps users informed during long runs, and asking for missing information avoids wrong actions based on guesses. Protocol hooks such as A2A Input Required and MCP elicitation exist for the second pattern. Silence and JSON input both hurt usability.
rationales: Structured tool input is the agent's job, not the user's.
Correct: streaming and step updates reduce perceived latency and add transparency.
Correct: clarifying questions prevent confident errors.
Long silent waits make users abandon or retry requests.

questions.scenario: An enterprise assistant started with 8 tools and now has 45 across HR, IT, finance and facilities. Tool-selection errors have risen sharply, and every new tool requires re-testing the whole prompt.
questions.stem: Which architectural change best restores accuracy and keeps the system maintainable as it grows?
options: Let the agent call tools at random and retry until one succeeds
Add more few-shot examples covering all 45 tools to the single prompt
Decompose into domain-specialist agents with small toolsets behind a router or supervisor
Switch to a model with a larger context window and keep one agent
questions.explanation: Capability decomposition keeps each agent's prompt and toolset small, which improves tool selection and lets teams test and change one domain without retesting everything. A router or supervisor dispatches requests. Bigger prompts and context windows do not fix the selection problem.
rationales: Random calls waste resources and can trigger unwanted side effects.
A longer prompt makes selection harder and testing heavier.
Correct: specialists with narrow toolsets scale in accuracy and maintenance.
Context size is not the bottleneck; choosing among many similar tools is.

questions.scenario: A platform team expects its agent service to grow from 50 to 5,000 concurrent sessions. Each agent process currently keeps conversation and orchestration state in memory.
questions.stem: Which change most directly enables horizontal scaling?
options: Make agent workers stateless and move session and checkpoint state to a shared external store
Pin each user to one large server for the life of their account
Increase the memory of the single agent process
Cache final answers in each process for one hour
questions.explanation: When state lives in a shared store, any replica can serve any request, so you can add replicas behind a load balancer and survive pod restarts. Vertical scaling and user pinning hit limits and lose state on failure. Per-process caches do not solve state placement.
rationales: Correct: stateless workers plus externalised state scale out cleanly.
Pinning creates hot spots and loses sessions when that server fails.
Vertical scaling has a ceiling and keeps a single point of failure.
Answer caching is unrelated to where conversation state lives.

questions.scenario: A team expects to change its LLM provider and add new frameworks over the next year. Today, model names, prompts and tool wiring are hard-coded across Python modules.
questions.stem: Which approach best improves the architecture's adaptability?
options: Fork the codebase for each provider
Freeze the current provider and framework to avoid change
Rewrite the agent in a single framework's proprietary format
Move models, prompts and tool wiring into versioned configuration and expose tools through stable interfaces
questions.explanation: Config-driven workflows and stable tool interfaces let you swap components without rewrites, and versioning them together allows evaluation and rollback. The NeMo Agent Toolkit follows this approach with YAML workflow configuration and plugins for multiple agent frameworks. Forks and lock-in reduce adaptability.
rationales: Forks multiply maintenance and drift apart.
Freezing ignores the stated requirement to change.
Proprietary lock-in makes future changes harder.
Correct: configuration plus stable interfaces makes components swappable.

sources.title: Agents and workflows — NeMo Agent Toolkit docs

questions.scenario: A coaching assistant holds sessions that last hours. Late in a session it forgets early goals the user set, and token costs climb with every turn because the full transcript is resent each time.
questions.stem: Which memory design best addresses both problems?
options: Keep resending the full transcript but switch to a cheaper model
Summarise or trim older turns in short-term context and persist key goals and facts in a long-term store retrieved when relevant
Start a new session every ten turns with no carry-over
Store every message in the system prompt
questions.explanation: Managing short-term context by summarising or trimming controls cost, while persisting important facts to long-term memory keeps them available beyond the context window. The study guide lists short- and long-term memory management under agent design. Dropping or stuffing history fails one goal or the other.
rationales: A cheaper model does not stop context growth or the forgetting.
Correct: bounded short-term context plus retrievable long-term memory.
Resets lose the goals the user cares about.
Putting every message in the system prompt is the same unbounded growth.

questions.scenario: A research organisation runs a supervisor agent that coordinates 24 specialist agents. The supervisor's context fills with worker outputs, it starts mis-routing tasks, and latency is high because every result returns to it.
questions.stem: What is the best architectural adjustment?
options: Give the supervisor a larger model and leave the structure unchanged
Run all 24 workers on every request
Introduce a hierarchical design: group workers into teams with their own supervisors that report summarised results upward
Remove the supervisor and let all 24 agents message each other freely
questions.explanation: Hierarchical orchestration limits how many workers and how much context each supervisor handles, and team supervisors summarise results before passing them up. A fully connected peer network is harder to control and debug. A bigger model does not remove the structural bottleneck.
rationales: The bottleneck is structural; a larger model just costs more.
Running every worker increases cost and context pressure.
Correct: team supervisors reduce the top-level fan-in and context load.
Free peer messaging among 24 agents makes coordination and tracing much harder.

questions.scenario: An order-status agent calls a shipping API that sometimes returns HTTP 503 for a few seconds. On each failure the agent's code retries immediately, up to 10 times. During a recent partial outage, thousands of sessions retried at once and the API took much longer to recover.
questions.stem: Which change best addresses the problem?
options: Remove retries and return the 503 error text to the user on the first failure
Raise the retry limit to 50 so each session has a better chance of eventually succeeding
Retry immediately but send the attempts in parallel so the user waits less
Retry transient errors with exponential backoff plus random jitter, and cap attempts and total time
questions.explanation: Retries without a delay, all landing at the same moment, create a thundering herd that slows recovery. Exponential backoff spreads retries out, jitter de-synchronises clients, and caps bound the cost. This is the transient-fault guidance in the study guide's Domain 2 readings.
rationales: Dropping retries gives up on faults that would clear by themselves and shows users raw errors.
More immediate retries put even more load on a service that is already struggling.
Parallel retries multiply the load instead of spreading it out.
Correct. Backoff with jitter and a cap is the standard way to handle transient faults.

questions.scenario: A retail assistant depends on an inventory service. The service went fully down for 25 minutes. During that time every user request waited through three retries, each ending in a 10-second timeout, before the agent gave up.
questions.stem: Which pattern would most directly prevent users from waiting on a dependency that is known to be down?
options: Increase the timeout to 30 seconds so slow responses have time to finish
Cache the LLM's system prompt to reduce token usage
Add a circuit breaker that opens after repeated failures, fails fast while open and serves a fallback
Add more retries with a longer backoff between them
questions.explanation: A circuit breaker notices repeated failures and moves to Open, where calls fail at once instead of waiting on timeouts. The agent can then serve a fallback. After a cool-down, Half-Open trial calls check whether the service has recovered.
rationales: Longer timeouts make users wait even longer for a service that is down.
Prompt caching has nothing to do with a dependency outage.
Correct. An Open breaker fails fast and makes room for graceful degradation.
More retries add delay and load during an outage. Retries suit transient faults, not long outages.

questions.stem: A circuit breaker protecting a document-search tool has been Open for its full cool-down period. What happens next under the standard pattern?
options: It sends traffic to the tool in alternate requests, half the time
It stays Open until an operator resets it by hand
It moves to Closed and sends all traffic to the tool again
It moves to Half-Open and allows a limited number of trial calls. Success closes it and failure opens it again
questions.explanation: After the cool-down, the breaker enters Half-Open and lets a few trial calls through. If they succeed it returns to Closed. If they fail it goes back to Open, which protects the dependency from a sudden flood of traffic.
rationales: Half-Open means a limited set of trial calls, not a 50% split of traffic.
The standard pattern recovers automatically. It doesn't need a manual reset.
Jumping straight to Closed risks flooding a service that may still be unhealthy.
Correct. Half-Open trial calls decide whether the breaker closes or reopens.

questions.scenario: A procurement agent has a create_purchase_order tool. Its HTTP client retries automatically on timeout. Finance reports duplicate purchase orders whenever the ERP system is slow: the first request succeeded, but the response arrived after the client timeout.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Turn off timeouts on the HTTP client so the first request always finishes
Send an idempotency key with each logical order so the ERP de-duplicates retried requests, and only auto-retry operations that are safe to repeat
Raise the retry count so the agent gets a confirmed response sooner
Tell the LLM in the system prompt never to call the tool twice
questions.explanation: Retries are only safe for idempotent operations. An idempotency key makes a non-idempotent write safe to retry, because the server recognises the duplicate. The duplicates here come from the client's retries, not the model, so a prompt instruction cannot fix them.
rationales: Removing timeouts can hang requests forever and still doesn't make writes safe.
Correct. Idempotency keys plus retrying only safe operations stop duplicate writes.
More retries would create even more duplicates.
The duplicates come from transport-level retries, not repeated model calls.

questions.scenario: An internal helpdesk agent uses a large LLM served from a NIM endpoint. The endpoint sometimes becomes unavailable for several minutes during maintenance.

Hand the conversation to a human agent with the conversation context attached
Fall back to a smaller model endpoint for simple requests while the primary is unavailable
Return the raw exception and stack trace to the user so they know what failed

rationales: Unbounded retries leave users waiting and add load. Retries must be capped.
Correct. A human handoff with context is a valid recovery path.
Correct. A simpler model keeps simple requests working during the outage.
Stack traces confuse users and can leak internal details.

questions.scenario: A research agent built with a ReAct loop calls a web-search tool. When the search tool raises an exception, the whole agent run crashes and the user gets a generic 500 error. Other tools that could answer the question are available.
questions.stem: What is the best way to handle tool failures inside the agent loop?
options: Leave the exception unhandled so monitoring picks up the crash
Remove the search tool from the agent so it can never fail
Catch the exception and return a structured error message as the tool observation, so the model can try another tool or re-plan, with a maximum number of iterations
Silently return an empty result so the model assumes there was no information
questions.explanation: In a ReAct loop, tool results come back to the model as observations. Returning a clear, structured error lets the model reason about the failure and choose another action, and the iteration cap stops endless loops. Empty results hide the failure and invite hallucination.
rationales: Crashing the run is the opposite of graceful recovery. Log the error and still recover.
Removing a useful tool sacrifices capability instead of handling errors.
Correct. A structured error as the observation allows recovery within bounded iterations.
Hiding the failure misleads the model and can lead to fabricated answers.

questions.scenario: A claims-processing assistant uses one 3,000-token prompt that extracts policy fields from an email, classifies the claim type, checks eligibility rules and drafts a reply. Failures are frequent and hard to diagnose, because nobody can tell which part went wrong.
questions.stem: What is the best redesign?
options: Remove the instructions about output format to give the model more freedom
Split the work into a prompt chain (extract, classify, check eligibility, draft) with schema validation between steps and routing based on the classification
Switch to the largest available model and keep the prompt as it is
Add more examples to the single prompt until its accuracy improves
questions.explanation: Dynamic prompt chains break a task into focused steps whose outputs can be checked before the next step runs. Routing on the classification adapts the flow at runtime, and failures can be traced to one step. A bigger model or a longer prompt does not give you either of those.

Correct. A validated, routed chain makes each step reliable and traceable.
A bigger model may help a little, but it doesn't make the system testable or traceable.
A longer single prompt stays hard to debug and keeps mixing several jobs.

questions.scenario: A partner company runs its own planning agent. It wants to hand off whole "reconcile this invoice batch" jobs to your NAT-based finance workflow and track them to completion. Your security team does not want to expose your internal tools or memory to the partner.
questions.stem: Which integration fits best?

Expose every internal tool to the partner through an MCP server
Publish the workflow through NAT's A2A server, so the partner's agent can delegate tasks without seeing your internal tools or state
Give the partner read access to your vector database

This exposes the internal tools security wants to protect. MCP connects agents to tools and data; agent-to-agent task delegation is what A2A is for.

Database access exposes data and doesn't delegate a task.

questions.scenario: A report-generation agent always follows the same pattern: look up the account, fetch the last quarter's metrics, fetch open tickets, then summarise. The team wants to cut latency and LLM cost. Tool results rarely change which steps come next.
questions.stem: Which agent strategy best fits?
options: A fully reactive agent with no tool use, answering from model knowledge
Several ReAct agents debating each step before any tool is called
A ReWOO-style agent that plans all tool calls up front, executes them, then synthesises the answer with fewer LLM calls
A ReAct agent that reasons after every observation before choosing the next tool
questions.explanation: ReWOO separates planning from execution. It plans the tool calls once, runs them, and makes a final synthesis call, which saves LLM round-trips when the sequence is predictable. ReAct's per-step reasoning is worth its extra cost when observations often change the plan. NAT offers both agent types.
rationales: Without tools the agent can't get account-specific data.
A multi-agent debate adds cost and latency instead of reducing them.
Correct. Planning up front cuts LLM calls and latency for predictable tool sequences.
ReAct adds an LLM call after each tool result, which is wasted when the plan is fixed.

questions.scenario: You are reviewing the resilience design for an agent's calls to a CRM API. The CRM sometimes returns 503 during deployments, and it occasionally has longer outages.
questions.stem: Which TWO design choices are correct? (Select two.)

Make the retry logic check the circuit breaker and stop retrying while the breaker is open
Reset the circuit breaker to Closed after each retry attempt so traffic keeps flowing
Retry only transient failures such as timeouts and 503s, not validation (400) or authentication errors
