Correct. Versioned configs let you know exactly which policy was in force for each response.
Audit data must be redacted and access-controlled. Open raw logs can leak PII.
Generated reasoning can be wrong or incomplete and doesn't prove which rails or tools ran.

questions.scenario: A product manager says the team doesn't need to plan for the EU AI Act yet because it is "only a proposal".
questions.stem: Which response is most accurate?
options: Correct. Nothing is binding until member states each pass their own AI laws
Incorrect. The Act applies only to model providers, never to companies deploying agents
Correct. It covers only biometric systems, so a support agent is out of scope
Incorrect. It is adopted law, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, with risk-based obligations such as transparency and human oversight phasing in

The Act's risk-based obligations are not limited to model providers.
Its scope is risk-based and broader than biometrics. Transparency duties can apply to conversational systems.

questions.scenario: A team wants one consistent safety policy (jailbreak detection, topic control and content safety) applied to three internal chat apps built by different groups.
questions.stem: Which architecture fits best?
options: Copy the same system prompt into each app and ask each team to keep it in sync
Run a shared NeMo Guardrails server with one config that uses the NemoGuard jailbreak, topic-control and content-safety models, and point all three apps at its chat completions endpoint
Fine-tune each app's model to refuse unsafe requests and remove runtime checks
Rely on each LLM provider's default moderation and add nothing else
questions.explanation: Running NeMo Guardrails as a server exposes an OpenAI-style chat completions endpoint, so several apps can share one versioned policy config. The NemoGuard models cover jailbreak detection, topic control and content safety as separate rails. Copied prompts drift, and fine-tuning alone gives up runtime, auditable enforcement.
rationales: Copied prompts drift between teams and are easily overridden. That's not enforceable policy.
Correct. A shared server with one config gives the same layered rails to every app.
Fine-tuning helps, but removing runtime checks drops a defence layer and the audit trail.
Provider defaults are not your enterprise policy and differ between providers.

questions.scenario: An operations agent can look up invoices, draft emails, and issue refunds through a payments API. Leadership wants human oversight without slowing down routine lookups.
questions.stem: Where should the team place a human approval gate?
options: Before the refund tool executes, showing the order and amount and letting the reviewer edit or reject it
On every tool call, including invoice lookups, so nothing runs unreviewed
After refunds are issued, in a daily report reviewed by finance
In the system prompt, instructing the model to double-check refunds before calling the tool
questions.explanation: Approval gates belong before side-effecting or irreversible actions, and the reviewer should see the concrete action and be able to edit or reject it. Gating every read-only call causes approval fatigue, and after-the-fact review cannot prevent harm. A prompt instruction is not an enforced control.
rationales: Correct: gates the irreversible, side-effecting step and shows the exact action.
Gating read-only lookups adds friction and leads to rubber-stamp approvals.
A post-hoc report detects problems but cannot stop a bad refund.
Asking the model to self-check is not enforced oversight; the orchestrator must pause.

questions.scenario: A LangGraph-style agent pauses for manager approval before provisioning cloud resources. Approvals often arrive the next day. Currently the worker process blocks while waiting, and when it is restarted the run starts over and re-creates a ticket it had already opened.
questions.stem: Which design best fixes both problems?
options: Increase the worker timeout to 48 hours so the process never restarts during a wait
Make the agent re-ask for approval every hour until the manager responds
Remove the approval step and rely on output guardrails to block risky provisioning
Interrupt the graph at the approval node, persist state to a durable checkpointer, and resume from that checkpoint when the approval arrives
questions.explanation: Interrupt-and-resume on checkpointed graph state frees the worker while waiting and lets the run continue from the approval node, so earlier side effects such as ticket creation are not repeated. Longer timeouts still lose state on restart, and removing the gate drops oversight entirely.
rationales: A longer timeout still ties up a worker and loses everything on any restart.
Repeated prompting adds noise and does not preserve state or prevent duplicate side effects.
Guardrails complement but do not replace human approval for high-impact actions.
Correct: durable checkpoint plus resume avoids blocking and avoids repeating side effects.

questions.scenario: A customer-support agent built from an NVIDIA blueprint answers billing questions using retrieval over policy documents.
questions.stem: Which escalation policy is most appropriate?
options: Escalate only when the user types the word 'human'

Escalate when retrieval returns no sufficiently relevant policy, when the request is high-stakes or repeated tool calls fail, or when the user asks, passing the conversation and tool results to the human
Never escalate; instead let the model answer from general knowledge when retrieval fails
Escalate every conversation longer than three turns, without passing context, so the human starts fresh
questions.explanation: Good escalation combines confidence, risk, failure and user-request triggers, and hands over full context so the human does not start from zero. Answering from general knowledge when retrieval fails invites hallucinated policy, and context-free handoffs waste the human's time.
rationales: A keyword-only trigger misses low-confidence and high-risk cases.
Correct: covers confidence, stakes, failure and user request, with a context-rich handoff.
Answering without grounding on policy questions risks fabricated answers.
Turn count is a poor proxy for need, and dropping context degrades the handoff.

questions.scenario: Product managers want users to trust a research agent's answers and to understand what it did on their behalf.
questions.stem: Which transparency approach best fits that goal?

Hide tool activity to keep the UI clean and show only the final answer
Show the plan, cite the sources used, list tool actions taken, and state uncertainty, while keeping full traces for operators
Display a fixed disclaimer that answers may be wrong

Hiding tool calls conceals side effects and undermines trust.

A generic disclaimer gives no insight into what the agent did or why.

questions.scenario: After launch, a team adds a thumbs-down button to its agent's chat UI. Three months later they have thousands of thumbs-down clicks but cannot tell what went wrong or reproduce any of them.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would most improve the feedback loop? (Select two.)

Fine-tune the model directly on every thumbs-down conversation
Remove the button because negative feedback is too noisy to use
Triage flagged runs regularly and add the confirmed failures to the evaluation dataset used before each release

Curating confirmed failures into the eval set and re-evaluating before release closes the data flywheel. Untriaged fine-tuning can amplify noise, and dropping feedback discards the signal.
rationales: Correct: reason codes plus trace linkage make feedback actionable.
Training on unlabeled thumbs-down data without triage can encode noise or bias.
Removing feedback throws away the main signal for improvement.

questions.scenario: Two agents collaborate over A2A. The remote agent cannot finish a booking task until the user chooses between two flight options.
questions.stem: How should the remote agent signal this?
options: Return the task in the Failed state with an error message listing the options
Pick the cheaper option automatically to avoid interrupting the user
Put the task in the Input Required state so the client can collect the user's choice and continue the same task
Mark the task Completed and ask the client to submit a new task with the choice
questions.explanation: In A2A, Input Required is an interrupted, non-terminal state designed for exactly this: the task pauses until the client supplies the missing input, then continues. Failed and Completed are terminal, and silently choosing for the user removes their oversight.
rationales: Failed is terminal; the work cannot continue on the same task.
Choosing without the user removes a decision that belongs to them.
Correct: Input Required is the protocol's HITL interrupt state.
Completed is terminal and misrepresents unfinished work.

questions.scenario: An auditor asks why an agent approved a large credit-limit increase last month. The team has application logs with the final answer but nothing else.
questions.stem: What should the team have recorded to make this decision traceable?
options: A trace of the run with spans for each LLM call, tool call, retrieval and guardrail check, including inputs/outputs, model and prompt versions, and any human approvals
Only the final answer and a timestamp, to minimize storage
The model's raw chain-of-thought text, which fully explains the decision
A weekly aggregate of approval counts per agent
questions.explanation: Decision traceability means a specific decision can be reconstructed: which steps ran, what data they saw, which versions were in use, which guardrails fired, and who approved. Final answers or aggregates cannot explain one decision, and raw reasoning text alone is neither complete nor guaranteed faithful.
rationales: Correct: per-step traces with versions and approvals let auditors reconstruct the decision.
Final answer plus timestamp is what they already have and it explains nothing.
Reasoning text omits tool data and versions and may not reflect the true cause.
Aggregates cannot explain an individual decision.
